THE SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Oral History
Interview with Theodore (Red) Saunders
Reel 1

Washington, D. C.
March 7, 1978

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
PROCEEDINGS
MR. DEMICHAEL: Part One, interview with Red Saunders, in his residence, 8134 South Evans Avenue in Chicago, Illinois 60619. March 7, 1978.
Okay, let's start at the beginning. When and where were you born?
Yeah, well, I was born in Memphis, Tennessee on March 2, 1912. Yeah, so --
When did you move to Chicago?
Well, I moved to Chicago in 1923.
When you were 11 years old.
Yeah, right.
Your family came up here.
Yeah, well, my sister raised me, you know. Earlier, my mother died, in 1919, and then my father, he left us and my sister raised me. So she became my mother and father.
How many were in your family?
There was six of us, two girls and four boys. Now, we have only one brother left, so now -- and it's he and I, you know.
Were you the youngest or -- ?
I was the youngest, right, right. And my brother is the oldest boy. And this home here is -- was my sister's and for the last three years, I -- four years, in
fact, I raised -- I took care of her until she passed, about a year and a half ago.
Why did you all move to Chicago? For work?
Well, it was for working conditions, yeah. And I was a youngster, and my sister brought my younger sister and myself here and she raised us, and then she went to work here, you know.
Let's see, and that was '23.

That was in 1923, and she was very, very light-completed, and she worked -- during those times, they weren't like they are now. So she passed -- you know, they call it passing, she passed for white. She passed for white for -- oh, I guess up until about 1940, from that time, over 20-some years, 25 years. And she raised me and sent me to Milwaukee to boarding school there, and my other sister grew up to get a job.
And so, we had been very close ever since. She was like a mother, like I said before, to me.
How much older was she?
Well, when she passed she was 79 years old. And that was two years ago. So she would have been 81 now.
So she was about 16 years older than you.
Right, right.
Well, what neighborhood did you grow up in?

Well, I would say that I'm really a true South Sider. I've lived all over the South Side. When we first come to Chicago in 1923, I lived on 43rd Street, 43rd near St. Lawrence. And then later years I moved to 65th Street, then I lived at 65th Street, and I just lived -- and my home over at 63rd and Ingleside and now I'm living here at 83rd, and then I had a home over on 73rd and Calumet. So I've lived practically all over the South Side. Right, right.
You said you went to a boarding school in Milwaukee. How old were you then?

Well, when I went to boarding school in Milwaukee, it would have had to be 11 or 12. It was in 1925, I think, I went there, about 1926, it was. 1926, right. And then I was there for two years. And that was St. Benedict's, at that time.
Catholic school.
Catholic school, right.
Are you a Catholic?
Right, right, right, uh-huh.
When did you start getting interested in music?

In Milwaukee, there. See, at the school, they wanted to start a band. So they just picked out the different kids and asked each one of them what instrument they wanted to play. And then they had an association with the Milwaukee Symphony. And so I took drums from this Symphony drummer in Milwaukee, and on Saturday afternoons, they would have class lessons. And they would charge ten cents a lesson for it.
So this is where I really got started.
Was this a marching band?
Well, yeah, it was a -- yeah, like a marching band, and a little concert band together.
And you wanted to play drums from the --
Right, right from the beginning.
Why did you want to play drums?
Well, I don't know. In the beginning, at home they said I had to be a drummer because I used to beat on pots and pans and all -- the fence and everywhere, you know?
Yeah?
Yeah, so, I mean, it was just an instinct, a feeling, you know?
Quinn Wilson -- I had one of these interviews with Quinn Wilson a few months ago, and he grew up in the same neighborhood as Lionel Hampton.
Right.
And he said Hamp used to do this before he started playing anything. He went around beating on curbstones and --

Right, right, right, right. And then, when we first come to Chicago, in -- around '23, was the heyday of Lil Armstrong, who was from Memphis, and she and my sister were very, very close friends there, they were real buddy-buddy girls.
Did your sister know Lil in Memphis?

Yeah, that's what I'm saying, in Memphis -- they went to school in -- elementary school together. All the way through school, and when I come here, then I stayed with them for awhile. We stayed with Lil and Louis. They had just gotten married. They got married in '24.
Yeah.
Uh-huh, and we stayed with them, you know, for awhile.
What do you remember from that time of living with Louis and Lil?

Well, during that time, they -- Chicago was such a musical town and there was so much music going on, and then they were working night clubs, you know, because she was in the Dreamland Cafe then. And so -
But she got the gig there and Louis came back --
And Louis -- yeah, and she met him and had to work with him.
Yeah.

Yeah, right, see, so their association -- I mean, I was just going to school and then I didn't have too much because they were working -- they would work til 3:00 or 4:00 in the morning, and then they got home, and then the musicians in those days were really happy-go-lucky guys. Maybe they'd get home at 12:00 and maybe not. But it was -- that was the earliest association with them, and then --
Do you remember Louis practicing or anything at home?
Not too much then, but I remember how he had to -- how he used to scuffle, and when he left the Savoy and then he had the Savoy Five, and they used to play these dances up at the Warwick Hall.
Oh, with Zutty [Singleton] and Earl Hines.
Right, Earl and Zutty, and they made classic records that they had made. Those are classics today.
Well, it was the avant garde of its time.
Right, right, right.
When Louis played, that was -- that's still some wild --
Right, right, right, right.
Well, let's go back to Milwaukee.
So they formed this band --
Yeah.
-- of school children, and you started playing snare drum, I take it.
Right, right, I was playing snare drum. Then we had a bass drummer, you know, and -- in the band, and I guess we had about 20 pieces, 18 or 20 pieces. It was a small brass band.
But -- and I started there, and then the sisters would teach us, too. They had some sisters there who formed a band who had musical experience. So that's how I got my start in the music then.
And you were -- what, 11, 12?

Right, it was around in there. Well, a little more than that, because, let's see, 1912 and then -- let's see, this was '26, about 14, and then I come out of the elementary school there, and then I come back to Chicago and went to Tilden Tech. So I -- and then I went in the band at Tilden Tech. And my first inspiration back there was the time when John Philip Sousa came in to direct the band, and man, that was really a real kick, you know.
And then when they would take us down to Orchestra Hall, and Frederick Stock was the conductor, then, so this is -- that was a little of the background of the music.
It must have been a heck of a band, the Tilden High School band?

Yeah, right, right. And at that time -- I don't know how -- but you know how the Board of Education, when they have something like Sousa or somebody would come around, they would expose him to the children, Yeah, so he came in and he directed the band and everything. It was a wonderful experience.
And that's always lived with me, all these years.
Who else was in that -- any fellows that went on to become professional musicians?

No, I lost track of a lot of them, because I didn't go all the way through high school. I left, and then I went travelling, I travelled an awful lot. First, before that I joined a guy around here called Stump King. And all the musicians -- see, in those days, things were really rough, they were really -- we're talking about, now, around '28. And back in there and right after that, the stock crashed and all of that.
And -- but the prohibition era -- prohibition wasn't repealed then, and so you still had these roadhouses and things that were run by the mob. And you would -- they would sell

moonshine and beer and all that. But they were all out in the suburbs. I mean, not suburbs, but out in the boondocks. And we used to -- this fellow -- this is all he did was to hustle. He would call it hustling. And he would --
You mean hustling gigs?
It wasn't a gig. What he would do, he would find a guy with a car, and then give this guy a percentage of what we were going to make that night. Nobody knew what we were going to make.
(unintelligible).

Yeah, and so we would go and get in these -- this automobile and he would go to -- he was a genius at finding these joints. I don't know how he knew about them, and then he would go in and ask them if they wanted some music. And then he would -- and they would say yes, he had a nice salesmanship about him, we would go in, then he'd pass the hat. And then we'd go -- after we were there about a half hour, and he'd got as much as he could get out of them, we'd jump in the car and go to another. And we'd get home about 8:00 or 9:00 the next morning because it's so far out, and you know how roads and things were then. We didn't have the super highways and all that that we have now. And, believe me, this guy had some of the greatest musicians that Chicago ever saw.
Well, was this the first regular band
Yeah, it was the first thing that I ever worked with.
And he was called the Stump?
No, his name was Stomp King.
Stomp King.

Yeah. Davis was his -- James Davis was his name, but he called himself Stomp King and he stuttered, and he was a nervous wreck and this type of -- but he -- things were just so pathetic at that time, because there was no work. Some of the guys or whoever in the radio stations and theatres and those things, but how many of them did the black musicians have back then? They didn't have too much.
They had a lot of black theatres.
Well, there was only a few of them that had music. The Vendome with Erskine Tate, and --
(Inaudible.)
No, the Regal didn't start until -- yeah, well, it started in '28, right, in '28. But it was just the thing, it wasn't enough to take the demand of how many black musicians there were.

I read a paper, a very interesting paper, on black music in Chicago in the '20s. And according to this researcher, it seemed to be divided into three levels. The highest level was the theatre musicians.
Yeah.
And the next highest level were the ballroom --
Yeah.
-- musicians. And then the lowest level were what they called the cabaret musicians, which a lot of these New Orleans jazz musicians came up from.
Yeah, right.
Were playing in cabarets, and were sort of looked down by the black musical establishment like Dave Peyton and --
Yeah, yeah.
Do you recall that? That's --

Yeah, right, right, yeah, right. Well, to a certain extent. See, it's like I say. You could categorize it like that, but there wasn't that much. Like, the Regal Theatre, now, they had a band. They had about a 12-piece band there. And maybe they would augment for particular shows or something. Dave Peyton was there with his -- he was the musical director. Then they had Sammy -- well, Fats Waller played there, played the organ.
And then Sammy Williams came in and he played the organ for years in there. And there, and then across the street, Sammy Stewart at one time played for the Metropolitan Theatre.
Metropolitan, that's --
Right, right, right.
Sid Catlett was in that band.
Yeah, right. See, but after that, you didn't have -- maybe you had a -- a lot of times they were playing -- they had musicians to play the picture, but maybe -- most of those just had piano players.
Yeah.
Now, you had the Grand Theatre, which was the Grand, and you had the Monogram. Now, but those theatres were TOBA,* and they used -- they'd say, what does TOBA mean? Tough On Black Acts.
I've heard it named Tough On Black Asses.
Yeah, yeah.
Tough on Black Actors.

Right, right, yeah. So, they had that, and -- but then they did more or less what they are doing today. A lot of them were self-contained, like when Ma Rainey would come in, Bessie Smith would come in.
They'd bring their own group.
They'd bring their own groups, like, -- guys like Fletcher Henderson and those kind of guys worked with a lot of those people. Louis played a lot of those things, but --
* TOBA - Theater Owners Booking Agency.
He made records --
Records, right, right, right, right.
When -- to go back for just a minute, when did you start playing a set of drums, rather than just snare drums?
Oh, I started then after I come out, and we started to go into hustling and things like this, then I started on the set of drums. There was no such thing as a sock cymbal back there, then.
(Unintelligible.)

Well, that came in later, it wasn't nothing. You just had that left -- that left foot was free. And then -- but like I was telling you, this guy -- boy, he had some of the best-- Omar Sim8on would go out on some nights, D Howard, he would go out some nights.

And any night, you could find -- meet some of the best musicians in the city of Chicago. They were just doing anything, and you'd pick up four dollars, five dollars and that was a good night.
Sure.
Right.
Well, did Stomp King, did he play an instrument?
He played a very bad piano.
Oh.
Yeah. And so, if they didn't have a piano, he would direct.
Would the band vary in size?
Yeah, right, whatever you could get.
Was it a fake band?
Right, fake band, yeah, right, right, yeah.
And what would it bring you, from three to six --
Three to four, five, six. Six was a big band.
What would you play?
Well, we played the tunes of the day then. A lot of the things like the New Orleans tunes and things like that.
But you were playing jazz.
Yeah, right, all jazz. It was all jazz.
Well, what happened after that, after those days of --

Well, after those days here, then I had an opportunity to get West, and so I went to -- with a little group, I went to Colorado. And a fellow had a big car, and -- see, when you put yourself in that era, you were just speculating. Everything was speculation, almost. So this guy

wanted us to go out West, and so we had about a four, five piece band. And he would go out to book some dances and things, and we had a few. And the next thing I know, he had one of those great big Pierce Arrows, at that time, with the headlights on side and all that. And he -- this thing caught afire and burned up. So that left us, so that blew that gig, because without any transportation out in New Mexico, where we were at that particular time, you --
So you played Colorado and --

Yeah, we played Colorado, well, this is -- the next state is New Mexico. And then -- so this was like a little territory thing that we were going to try to build up. But nothing really happened behind that.
Whose band was that?
This was just a pickup group, just a pickup group.
Who was the leader?
Let's see, a fellow by the name of Roosevelt Thomas, out of St. Louis. And he went out with us, you know.
He was the one that had the Pierce Arrow.
No, another fellow and his wife, yeah. He had the Pierce Arrow and so it was the same type of a deal as I had just left.
When was this, about '29?

Yeah, this was -- no, I would say this would -- say about 1930, '31, and it was really rough, really rough. So then, I met some musicians from Pueblo, Colorado, and so they formed a little band, so I worked with them for awhile. A fellow by the name of Belton Everett. And I worked with him, because there was another saxophone player in the town, so they took the rhythm section and some others, and we worked with them around Pueblo and all of that. And he gave us a place to say and things like that.

And then I finally found that I had an auntie there, and she worked for a country club, so I didn't have to worry about nothing to eat. I was straight there, you know. So after I left -- I mean, I stayed there, and then finally I got ajob with the Walkathons. Remember the Walkathons?
Sure, sure, I remember the Walkathons.

Yeah, so we went to Denver, and they had the Eligious Garden, I think it was,that they had the Walkathon, and I went to work there with a fellow with a fellow named Ira Coffee. He was a piano player. And I stayed with the Walkathon for about three or four years.
Piano and drums?
No, it was piano, drums and saxophone and he got a fellow out of -- who's still in Dixieland, a great Dixieland player, now he's in St. Louis, Norman Mason. He was
in the band, and we had -- I can't remember who -- oh, yeah, a fellow by the -- I can't think of his name, a good trumpet player. He was out of St. Louis. And Coffee was out of St. Louis.

So I travelled with them, because each state we would maybe stay six months. And we stayed in Denver, we went to Minneapolis, Atlantic City and Kansas City. And in Kansas City, when we were there, we got a young comedian out of the burlesque and that was Red Skelton. That was one of his first jobs, and he stayed with them until -- oh, he stayed with them about two or three years.
Well, did the Walkathons have sort of shows?

Right. Actually what it was was the contestants did singing and different things like -- but they would have MC's, see. And these MC's, like, Red was a comedian, but he was an MC, too, and they had Dick Buckley -- I don't know whether you remember him. He was around here at one time, Dick Buckley. Well, he was one of the comedians, and MC's.
So that was the way, and then the contestants did most of the entertaining, and they had the band there.
Yeah, I barely remember one in Louisville, Kentucky.
Right.
Where I was born and raised.
Yeah, right.
It was out in Terry Park. And this must have been '36. I would have been about eight, then.
Right, right, uh-huh, right, right, that's right.
But it was a strange phenomenon of the time.
Oh, right, but -- they were going to go watch them walk, but, see, they had this thing where they were drooping, and then they had sponsors. They had the different merchants were sponsors. And --
That's right. (Inaudible) rode on their back.
Rode on their back, right, right. And they --
(Unintelligible.)

Right, but they had it built up where they -- when they went on the air, they were broadcasting, and when they went on the air, this was the thing whether they were pulling for this couple and blah blah blah and everybody screaming, and it was -- it created excitement.
Yeah. Same days of the flagposts.
Right, right.
Trying to make some money.
Right, right, right, right.
So you were in the Walkathon for about four years, you said?
Yeah, I was in there about four years, yeah, right. And then -- but the Walkathons, I -- they were -- paid good money, of that day, during that day.
Sure.
I was making about $55 dollars a week, of $50-some, come from --
That was a good salary.

-- hustling to this. This was a great -- and when I played Kansas City, this was a great -- see, we got a chance to move around, and when I went to Kansas City, Basie and them were starving. Basie, George [E. Lee].
(Simultaneous discussion -- unintelligible.)

Well, they were -- we were all hanging out -- right, no, this was just before the Orange Blossom, just before. We were living at 18th and Vine, then. It was a hotel there, and the guys used to just hang out there, and, man, all the musicians in the world, they all loved each other, though.
Was there such a person as Piney Brown?
Oh, yeah, he was one of the biggest pimps. Piney Brown, he was one of the biggest pimps. I lived
about three doors from him in the hotel.
Really?
On the same floor. Right, right, Piney Brown.
"Piney Brown's Blues".

Right, right, right, right, yeah, see, so Piney and -- he was living there, and Jesse Stone was living there, Vic. Dickenson had just come. They had -- when I was there, I was there for about six months, and during this six months was the time when Benny Morton's band and Thamon Hayes -- see, Benny Morton had had a summer job at the Fairlen Park every year. And this year, Thamon Hayes got the job, see, and Thamon Hayes used to be with George Lee. And so he formed a band and he took half of Benny's band. And they formed a band to go to Fairlen Park.
And then -- what's his name, Benny Morton sent and got Ben Webster. Ben Webster came to Kansas City and he was there playing, Lester Young was with George Lee at that particular time.
You know, Ben and Prez were sort of childhood chums.
They were, yeah, right, see, and then when they come to Kansas City there, Kansas City was such a musical town --
When was this, about '32?
'32, right, this is in '32, right. And so --
Morton had a hell of a band. His records, 'Morton Swing' and --
Oh, yeah, right, right, all of that, yeah. Look, he had Hot Lips Page in his band, he had Eddie Durham in his band, his brother Bus Morton was in the band, he was a conductor for the band.
Well, Basie worked in that --
And Basie played in the band, right. See, Bus was a piano player, but he played accordion instead -- and Basie was playing piano. And, see, like I told you, in this hotel -
(Unintelligible).
Yeah, and all these musicians gathered around in this hotel. And if they didn't live there, it was their meeting place.
What was the name of the hotel, do you recall?
Booker T.
Booker T.
Booker T Hotel, right.
Not Booker T. Washington, but Booker T.
No, Booker T. We just called it the
I guess maybe it was the -- but I never did know anything but Booker T.
And then, across the street was the Cherry Blossom, but it wasn't the Cherry Blossom, it was a theatre at that time, but right -
The Cherry Blossom or the Orange Blossom?
The Cherry Blossom.
The Cherry Blossom.
Then, see, then right after this time, see, because this was the beginning of the demise of Benny Morton's band.
Right.
And then the Cherry Blossom opened up. I had just left, and then Basie organized his bands, started his band there.
Right, out of Morton band.
Right, right.
When you were in Kansas City, you mentioned, Vic Dickenson was down there, and I interviewed Bing one time, he was telling me about the sessions.
Oh, listen --
Did you ever go to the sessions?
Oh, man, that was the thing. Do you know, if anybody would come to Kansas City at that time, and

was reputed to be a great saxophone player or a great horn player, they would dig all over town or send a cab after and bring somebody down there to give you a fit. And this is what I was saying about Ben and Lester, see, and if some other saxophone -- Joe Massick came down there one time.
Yeah?

This was when Joe was playing -- he was a great player, he would play -- he was with Tweet Ogen's band. I don't know whether you remember it. But, anyway, they came back -- so he come down on 18th Street, and so they finally -- they sent all over town to get Lester, see, because Ben and he had been tying up there, so Ben went over to the piano, see, playing chords, and Lester and --
And Joe --

Joe tied up. And this is the type of a thing that would go on day after day. And if there was a trumpet player, they'd go send and get some of the -- Hot Lips Page or they would go and send -- get Paul Webster or somebody like that.
Yeah.

Pardon me. So that was -- that was the way these sessions -- and then, they had a battle of bands in there. See, Benny Moten's band would play at the Harlem and they would have Duke Ellington's band. And then it was one of those things where -- you know, and Benny and them --

Benny Moten's band was the greatest band for just sitting down -- and they would start off a tune, this was tunes like "Moten's Swing" and all those things. And then they'd start to setting these riffs.
Yeah.
And this is where Basie got that thing, from "One O'Clock Jump." But he used to call that Old Babe, you know what I mean? And that was just a riff, you know?
You know Zilner Randolph?
Yeah, Z.T.
Well, he told me about that bit. He claimed that it came from Louis Armstrong's recording of Stardust, when Louis sang, oh, memories, oh, memories.
Uh-huh, but that was a --
Who knows?
Who knows? It was a standard riff back there, and they would go (singing), but it was that thing. And then Basie finally put it in that "One O'Clock Jump".
Well, did you play in some of the sessions? Did you sit in --
Oh, yeah, right. And there was a first time -- we were talking about the sock cymbal?
Uh-huh.
That was the first one down on the floor. Yeah, right, right, right.
Yeah. I had an old low hat one time. I wish I had of kept it.
Yeah, right, right, right, right.
First set of drums. During the war, you couldn't get a --
No, no, right, right.
So they had this old low hat in --
Right, and it had a thing like a (unintelligible), and then you put your foot on the wood and then a spring, (laughter.)
I wish I'd kept that thing.
Yeah, right, right.
Just as an artifact.
Uh-huh.
Well, Jo Jones was playing then. Was he playing --
No, I didn't meet Jo back in there. I didn't meet -- you know who I -- Baby Lovett.
Right.
Baby Lovett, Julia Lee, Mary Lou Williams, all the greatest array of -- and it was the greatest array of musicians in the world. Right there.
That's right.
You know? And what they would do, like I said, the guys would come in, they would sit up in the
lobby, and at 11:30 -- I guess it was 11:30 at night, that lobby would be full, listening to Earl Hines, coming from the Grand Terrace.
Yeah.
Right, see, so --
Where did these sessions take place in Kansas City?

They -- in a little joint called the Subway. And it was down in the basement, it was down in the basement. It was a restaurant on top of something, and then right down in the basement, they had this subway. It was like a little club, a little club. And this is where they would take place.

And I saw Basie about -- this was about a year ago, now, I don't know if he wants it repeated. This is an in thing, we were sitting up talking, and I said, 'do you remember Slam Foot? That was a piano player and he used to play a lot of the sessions. He said, 'man, you would be the only one in the world that would know something like that, yeah.' And then this was when he organized his band. And the funniest thing, boy, -- you know Willie Berg?
No.
Hums and Berg, you know, the instrument people? All of these are different stories. I may be getting away --
Oh, no, keep --

Well, Willie Berg at that time was a little young Jewish -- he tried to play clarinet. But what he did, he had a kit about this big. And he'd put reeds and he'd put all of these -- and for years, he would go around with these things to the different clubs and the different places and things. And he would sell them.
He was a peddler.

Yeah, he was a peddler. But the guys were always glad to see him, because when he would walk in, the drummer always needed a pair of sticks, a guy would need a pair of reeds -- I mean, some reeds and things like that. And he -- I can't think of who it was, but it was some prominent musician, and he was saying -- and so he would give these guys these things, and maybe the bill would run to 80 cents, and the guy would say, come back and see me in two weeks. So those were the things that were happening during those -- some of the things, right.
Well, where did you go after Kansas City -- and then you started with the Walkathon.

I was with the Walkathon. And then, see, in Kansas City, I was one of the highlights of the early bringing up in the music business. Because, I mean, you get -- not so much musically, but a true experience of life and things from guys like Vic Dickenson, and the guys who were

drinking-- see, they were heavy drinkers back in those days. They used to drink -- and we had a place right next to the hotel, it was a bootblack stand, and it was built like one of these train cars. And we would go in there and we would get our bootleg whisky, 25 cents a pint -- I mean, 50 cents a pint and 25 cents a half pint.

And many a day, Basie and all these guys got each a bottle. So by me making this kind of money, man, we would -- I'd come down, meet ten guys down there, we'd go to the show, 15 cents, dollar and a half.
So that was the kind of the spirit. But if you played music there, it was almost like New Orleans. Everybody loves a musician, a guy who can play. Yeah.
Well, in the Walkathon, was that sort of like your first show experience?
That was -- well, to a certain extent.
Because it was pretty low level.

It was low level, but right after I left the Walkathons, and this was about 1933 I left the Walkathons, pardon me, then I joined a big show, a big revue, called the Harlem Scandals. And there was a road show, and we travelled. We travelled all over.
How did you get that gig?
I had just come back to Chicago, and they needed a drummer. This was Curtis Mosely's band, and
Curtis Mosely had had a hell of a band at one time out of Los Angeles. And so they needed a drummer. Because he played drums himself, but he was pretty much over the hill at that particular time.

So they needed a drummer, so I joined them. And chorus girls, 20, 15 chorus girls, and all this type of a thing, and all the different dance teams and acts, big time acts, acts that had played the RKO vaudeville circuit and all of that, Norman Thomas' Quintet, and they had very good acts. And then the show things, and so this was really my introduction to shows, see, then with the big show, we played the Strand and Lake Theatre here in Chicago. We played the Old Stratford Theatre, I don't know whether you remember that, on 63rd Street. And it was a vaudeville house, then. And we played quite a few theatres here in Chicago.
But where -- you say you went on the road with it.

Well, we played everywhere. We played -- well, we played Indianapolis, and then through the state, and then we played the Butterfield Time, that was through the state of Michigan. And then we went West and -- we played practically -- mostly -- most of it was done in the Middle West.
But I was with them about a year, a year and a half.
Was that a big band, or --
Yeah, yeah, he had a big band. It was about 13 pieces. That was big at that particular time.
Did the band have a spot in the show?

Yeah, we did everything, the band did a spot. And then, they had big production numbers. They had a number in there, and it rained on the stage. They had -- they put the tarpaulin in there and then they had a line that they run over the top, then they spotlighted it, and this guy would be singing, 'oh, Lord, please take away the darkness,' and all of that, 'oh, please, take away the rain.' And then it would be raining. It was real first class.
Big production, yeah.
Real big production things. And that was my first introduction. And, young -- you have no fears, you don't know whether you can do anything or not, but you say you can. So I --
Were you reading then?
Yeah, right, right. Well, you have to -- I had to learn to read, right, right, right. So -- and the band was -- practically the whole band was out of California.
(Recording interrupted.)
Okay. So you started -- that's when you started playing shows.
That's when I started doing shows. That was my first introduction. And so I really didn't --
really wasn't -- it wasn't a gradual thing. I was just thrown into -- the rabbit in the briar patch.
Yeah, that happened to me, too. I was playing in this band, we got a show, and there was a pretty tough show --
Right, right, right, right.
Really screwed up. So I got me a job in a strip joint.
Yeah, right.
And learned to play shows. And by the time I left Louisville, I was --
Yeah, right.
I was one of the guys they called when they had a job to play.
Right. And then after that I played many a nightclub, but they were all joints to me. I had really cut my teeth already, so it was no problem anymore.
Yeah. Buddy Rich made a very nice statement in a recent DownBeat, that when he played Chicago, he'd always get out to DeLisa to watch you play the show.

Yeah, right, right. And he used to come out -- but -- and I remember it so much. And I had a picture, but I turned a lot of valuable and beautiful pictures over to the Chicago Historical Society. And I think they've got this picture of Buddy and myself in there, and then he was a young guy and I was real young. And that was some years ago,
yeah.
I remember those pictures in DownBeat of you for -- what was it, Slingeland
Yeah, Slingeland Drum Company, yeah, right, yes, sir.
(Recording interrupted.)
and T! S! P! 1
Talking about show drumming, and that's a specialty and you got into it --
Yeah, right, right
-- saying you could do it and had never done it before.
Right, right. And like I say, after cutting my teeth on this big show, then everything else came very easy, you know?
That's right.

And so then -- and now we're talking about 1933, around that time, see. And first the beer gardens came in. This was before hard whisky. And so all over town they opened up beer gardens, and you had to have some music. And they had little shows, and then they had the little bands and things, and not much money. We were just coming out of the Depression.
But it didn't cost much money to live, either.
(Inaudible.)
Right, right.
Chicago seems to always -- at least in the '20s and '30s, always seemed to be shows connected with the clubs. I know Quinn was telling me that all the places --
Yeah.
-- where the jazz historians say -- King Oliver played here, --

Right, right, but they had big shows, right, right, and Earl Hines, all those years at the Grand Terrace. Shows, but they had a outlet so that they could play their music, because a lot of them were broadcasting and things like that. They had to play dance music and things like that.

So a band playing in one of those places, they had to be very, very versatile. And -- I keep getting back to Basie, and -- like I told you about this thing, about Basie and this Willie Berg. Anyway, I was talking about him and he was telling me about when they were in the Grand Terrace, had just come out of here from Kansas City.
(Inaudible) the show.

No, no. And Basie would say, he used to come out there to the De Lisa, and he'd say, man, he was just amazed, his eyes would pop open. Then he'd go back and everybody -- because, nobody spoke to him, the waiters didn't speak to him.
Yeah, that was a pretty disastrous gig.

Right, right, right. And then the funny thing about it, -- and you know how musicians kid and things, and I said, Basie, you come here with that big raggedy band and that cold winter, and yo guys had those little trench coats on, and this weather was beating you to death. He said, that's right, right.

And then Willie Berg said -- Fox, who was the owner of the Grand Terrace called him up: "You've got to come here and get me some drums for this guy." Jo Jones had a snap drum and was sitting up on a -- this is what we used to do, though, didn't have no -- were so poor you didn't have no stand. You had a chair and you played -- (laughter.)
And you tilted on the chair.
Right, right. No sock cymbal at that time, and you had to tilt the chair, and he had these raggedy drums, so Fox told him, you got these things ruining my club. Yeah.
Then you heard the band when he was here.

Yeah, right, right. But, I mean, they were playing things -- they played Lester and all those guys in the band. But they just hadn't had the experience. See, because this was in Chicago, see, and then down there, they were jazz players. And they hadn't had any shows until Basie went in the Cherry Blossom and the shows that they had there
then were very mediocre.
Yeah.
And then they'd run into these big stars out of New York and thing like that. They had a night club circuit, you know.
(Inaudible.)
Yeah, right, right.
Yeah, Chicago was a lot different from Kansas City in those days.
Oh, yeah, in those days, right, right. But so far as jazz is concerned, they had some of the greatest jazz musicians in the world congregated there.
Right.
Right.
Well, they had some jazz musicians here, too.

Oh, there's great ones here. You had them down there, but, see, they were like second city or third city or whatever you wanted to call it. But they respected Chicago because they would sit there and listen and every -- ape and everything, because you had Louis Armstrong, Earl Hines and you had all kinds of great musicians. Omer Simeon, like we were saying, and Darnell Howard and Jabbo Smith and all the --
(Inaudible) Jabbo?
Yeah, yeah, right.
Hell of a trumpet player.
Yeah, he's still up in Milwaukee.
Yeah. Yeah, I heard him a couple of years ago, here in town with a college band that was sort of recreating Fletcher Henderson arrangements.
Yeah, right, right.
And his chops were down, but his --
But you still know he could play.
Beautiful ideas.
Yeah, right, right.
Gee, he used to be fa
Oh, he was fabulous.

Yeah, well, I was going to tell you. Louis Armstrong was playing in Carroll Dickerson's band, Tubbie Hall and all of them were over here in Clarence Black's band. And this guy came in -- I don't know where, didn't even know him. Boy, and he started blowing that horn, boy, and sweat come over Pop's -- and he was -- and that was one of the greatest nights I think I've ever heard of a rivalry. I

mean, it was a real rivalry, yeah. Right, because he sat in Clarence Black's band, Jabbo did, and then Louis, who naturally, you know -- and boy, that was really something. And he was playing then, Jabbo was.
Oh, yeah, Jabbo --
And this is really what -- that was my first introduction to him, you know.
Ira Sullivan used to be a neighbor of mine (inaudible).
(Recording interrupted.)
And Ira came over to my house one day.
Yeah.
And I said, did you ever hear of Jabbo Smith? He says no, so I put on this old Jabbo Smith record, the Boston Scuffle.
Yeah.
And Ira just fell on the floor.
No kidding.
He didn't know anybody played like that. He was playing bebop.

Right, right, right, and he -- on that particular night, you know, I mean, it was just such an intense rival and he was intent on showing his ability, and this guy after playing all of that, he picked up the trombone, man, and started playing, and played the hell out of it.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Too bad there weren't tape recorders back then.
Oh, yeah, right, right, right.
In Kansas City with those sessions.
Yeah.
So you came back to Chicago and you went with this -- with the Harlem Scandals?
Yeah, well, I travelled with them. We didn't locate anyplace, you know.
Yeah.

And I travelled with them, and so finally, I come back to Chicago and I had my first night club job. It was called the Club Annex. And it was with Jimmy Cobb. I don't know whether you remember Jimmy Cobb --
Jimmy Cobb.
Yeah, right.
Jimmy Cobb and Junie Cobb.

Junie Cobb, right. But Jimmy had the band, and I joined him, and that was when Leon Washington and Gaby Rogers, the piano player, and I don't know who was playing bass at that time, I can't think. But, anyway, that's when I worked with Chippy Hill and Billy Mitchell and all these people,

in this little night -- that's when I was telling you about the night clubs they had. But this was a nice little club, at 23rd and State Street. And I stayed there for about a year or so, and later, Benny Washington replaced me. You remember Benny Washington?
I remember the name.
The name, right, right. He replaced me there, and then I went on to --
Was that your home band?
No, no, that was Jimmy Cobb's band.
Jimmy Cobb's band, yeah.

Yeah, then I went on to gigging, jobbing, you know. That's when I worked with Tiny Parham, yeah, and he had a band in the Savoy Ballroom, and see, every night had gone, we worked Saturdays and Sundays and different nights in the Savoy Ballroom there.
Was this a big band?
Yeah, this was a big band.
Was the Cobb band a big band?
No, the Cobb band was a combo. That was about six pieces, night clubs and small clubs and that was --
What kind of music were you playing? I don't mean for the acts, but for the dancing or --
Well, we were playing jazz, all jazz.
Swing style.

Right, everything was -- they hadn't -- right at that time, they hadn't really categorized anything because this was the time right around this time, was when Benny Goodman started in the Congress Hotel down there. And then they started calling it Swing, right.

So that's where -- we started from there. But this night club, we played all kind -- we had a little line of girls, four girls or five girls. Little productions. But I had -- just like I said, I was straight, because I knew what I was doing then.
Did any particular drummers fascinate you or influence you?

Yeah, well, really, one of my favorites -- I mean, one of my real favorites was Big Sid Catlett, and I used to be amazed at Big Sid Catlett. This great, big 240 pounds -- or 45 or whatever, six-foot three of whatever he was, big man. And he had a touch on a drum that was phenomenal. It looked like he was playing with feathers. He was just -- and I always admired that in him.
You still remind me of Sid Catlett.

Oh, yeah, well, -- but I idolized him so, you know? And then in the years a little later on, it was Chick Webb. I listened to Chick. But Sid and I, we grew up -- Sid is a Chicago boy, and he grew up around here, and we were kind of buddy-buddy then. And that was really one

of the great things about musicians then. You were just like a brother. It didn't matter how much you played, you could hobnob with the greatest guy in the world, and never any inflection of your ability.
Yeah.
Right, and so it was really great then.
Real brotherhood.

Yeah, real brotherhood, right. And that's what I liked -- I told you about Kansas City. You played there, everybody loved you. And then, this town was the same way. The guys like Louis Armstrong, that was a great sight. Louis Armstrong and Earl Hines and all of these guys out in the Washington Park out there, playing baseball, with his big fat self. And it was real joy and they were getting real kicks out of it, a musicians' thing.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Those days are gone now.
Oh, yeah, right, right, right.
Maybe we need some more hard times or something.
Oh, yeah, right, because in later years, in the later years, we played softball, when I was at the Delisa and we would get off at 6:00 in the morning, and
then go change clothes and go out to the park and play softball. And we played teams like Woody Herman and they would get up in the morning and come on out and play.
All the bands had --
Right, all of them had a softball team.
Yeah.
Right.
Well, when did you go into the Delésá?
I went into the Delésá in '37.
Were you the leader then?

No. When I first went into the Delésá, Albert Ammons had just left, see, and they let him go because he couldn't play -- he couldn't read, see, and shows and things got the best of him. And then right after that, John Hammond -- he and --
Lux Lewis.
Lux and T. Johnson, teamed them up, [Delbert] and a boy by the name of Dell Bright was the saxophone player.
I know that name.

Yeah, so he had the band. And I stayed there about -- oh, six months or nine months, and then Dell went to work with Horace Henderson at the Swingland, and he went there because -- I guess he wanted a big band thing,

and Horace had a big band and we had only six pieces there. So he turned the band over to me. So I took the band over there, then in 19-- well, I guess about '37, '38, because I'd been there about -- the last part of '37, I think it was. And that's when I took the band over there.
It was a small band. We had only six men, trumpet, tenor, alto, bass, piano and drums, right.
What kind of club was it?

Well, it was a black and white -- a black and tan, they called them. And during those years, there was no color barrier or anything, and the whites would come to the South Side and feel free, and there was no mugging or none of that stuff going on. And they had full protection when they come into the club.
Now, the club was at 55th Street on the west side of the street, and it was --
55th-and --
And State.
And State.

And State, about four, five doors from the corner. Now, when the club first opened up, it opened up as a bar, and they had a band sitting up in the little balcony playing. So that was the beginning. And then they just added another part onto it, next -- in the lot next to it. And this started the Del-sa, and the further back you'd

go, the lower the ceiling would get. So you ended up bending down. And that was another high point, because the musicians used to come, like, every Monday morning for the breakfast show and all the performers from all over the city -- you don't know, you would meet people like Bob Hope, and then Buddy Rich was talking about it in his article. And you just didn't know who you would meet in there. All the musicians from all of the things, and then, way in the back back there they used to get in the back and the lights were down dim and everything, and nobody's sitting back there, and so you'd go back there and they'd blow the gage.
So it was just that wild, and they didn't pay any attention to it, nobody said anything. So --
Who owned the place?
Mike Delisa, and it was he and some brothers. And they owned it.
Was that a syndicate joint.
Well, really, you couldn't tell. Actually, I think, yeah, it was, right.
(Inaudible.)

Yeah, right, right, right. See, and then in '43 it -- the joint burned. In -- no, '41, I think it was, 1941, it burned down. That one on that side, so they rebuilt across the street, and then they built a stage with the -- hydraulic stage, and all of that.
And then they had -- the other place used to seat about 300. (It) would seat about 800.
This was about the time that -- the place where Earl Hines played.
The Grand Terrace.
Grand Terrace, when that sort of went down.

It was getting ready to go into a demise then. See, I don't know, the Grand Terrace thing, it was -- see, people then didn't -- we weren't in any prosperous area -- I mean, era, at that time. We weren't in a prosperous era, and their prices, I think, were a little high and -- because, at the Del'esa, this is what attracted so many people to it. You could come in there and get a setup, a setup would be ice and your Cokes and a couple of root beers or something like -- I mean, not root beer, ginger ale. And you'd get that a bring a half a pint of whisky and two people could get in there for two dollars.
Yeah.

And then more people, and it would add up. But it wasn't no strain on the pocketbook. And then it had a different atmosphere to it. They had little knockers, and they'd beat on the tables because they didn't have the tablecloths, just a plain -- tables, and they would beat on the tables and it was just a rollicking time.
What were the hours?
Well, during the weekdays, we'd go to work at 10:00 or 10:30 and we got off at 6:00.
Eight hours.
Right. And then on Sundays, during the club season, we would go to work at 5:00 in the evening and get off at 8:00 the next morning.
The club season, what --

I mean, what I'm saying, the club -- the social clubs, they would have the affair in there, they would take the club for maybe three or four hours. And if they started at 5:00, they would get out about 9:00. Then we would take a breather for one hour and so then we would come back, and then the night sessions started.
And then, after 4:00 or 5:00 in the morning, we would take another little break, and then the breakfast show would start.
We used to work a 12-hour gig down in Louisville on Sunday. We'd have a Sunday afternoon session and then we'd have a couple hours off to eat.
Yeah, right.
And then the regular gig started with the shows --
Yeah, right, right, right.
And playing at 2:00 in the morning.
Right, right, right.
That's when we were both younger.
Yeah, right, right, you had to be. You couldn't have made it, otherwise.
Well, how many shows were there a night?
Well, usually, it was three shows during the weekdays and four shows on Saturdays and Sundays. Yeah.
And how big were the show? Were they as big as the Grand Terrace?
Oh, yeah, right, right. They went up to as high as about 16 girls at one time.
Really?
They had 16 girls and they would have five and six acts.
Were these name acts?

Well, they were name acts -- they were name acts like today, with guys like Billy Eckstine, But, see, it was a proving ground for all these acts. They were young. See, we're talking about the '40s and things like that then, you know. Billy Eckstine, he got his start there, and George Kirby was -- at that time, he was a busboy there. And we wrote his first music and got him started. And Lurlene Hunter and LaVerne Baker and -- there's

I managed Joe. And, see, and he worked in the show. And I managed him for five years.
Well, where did you find him?
Well, Joe had been singing with --
He'd been around --
He'd been around here, right, he worked with Jimmy Noon, he worked with Andy Kirk's band, and then he had some problems. This can be restricted, because maybe he doesn't want it known.
Emotional problems?

Yeah, emotional problems, and he was a little off, to a certain extent. And then he gave up the singing and he couldn't get a job. And so then he was down by the Savoy, he was selling -- I mean, working in a hamburger joint, and then later he went to work for Fuller Products.
Fuller Brush?
Yeah -- no, no, Fuller Products, he was selling cosmetics and things like that.
Oh.
Then he started coming around the club because he was selling lipstick and things like that to the girls in the chorus. So when he would come around there,
then at that time, I had just gotten a contract with Columbia, and at that time, the big companies like Columbia and all of them, they --
When was this?

This was 195-- around -- see, because when I put that 'Hambone' out, that was in 1952. See, so in -- pardon me, this was during that time. So we -- I had some tunes and things, and I asked Jimmy if he wanted to make a session with us and he did. And that was -- and then, in the club, every day the thing that really set him off, well, this is where he created it, right there in the club. That was his big thing, that was his --
(inavudable) blues.
Yeah, what's his name --
Big Joe Williams.
No, no, Slim -- Memphis Slim.
Memphis Slim?
Memphis Slim was the first one that started singing, and then later B. B. King made it.
Yeah.
Yeah, right. That was Memphis Slim's number.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Well, let's go back to when you
first took over the band. You said it was a six-piece band.
Yeah, right, right.

Oh, yeah, we had everything then.

And then, the show, they had their own arranger for the show. He would come in and rehearse with them, and then write a thing. What's his name was one of the guys that wrote -- I mean, put the music together, Sonny Blunt was his name, Sun Ra.
Oh.
Yeah, right. Sonny Blunt was his name then. Then he changed, and --

Every three weeks.
Every three weeks you'd have a new --
New show.
New chorus.
Right, now routines, everything, a new show.

Yeah, well, eventually as the club -- the club was large.
After the first one --

Oh, right, right, right, right, right.

Oh, down on Randolph?
Randolph Street. Sonny was with me then. Yeah, right.
I remember that.
Yeah, right.
I came up from Louisville when I was about 16, and walked up and down --

That's where he learned how to play.
Right. And then Farnum, Dennis
Farnum.

Right.

Yeah, right, right, and he --
Nice player.
Nice fellow, nice player.

right. I don't remember all of the sides, but these are a few of them.

That was before I --
Yeah, oh, yeah, it was war years. And I worked with him in there, and then I --

[Brooks Kerr]

Right, right.
