-- power, and the Chicago Historical Society wanted to do a series of historical jazz concerts. I was the narrator and arranged for the bands. And we wanted to use black and white musicians. But since -- and it was a trust fund.
Right, yeah.
From Local 10.
Right, right.
And they said, you must use Local 10 musicians. We wanted to use Local 208, also.
208, right, right.
Also. Can't do that.
No.
They would not allow --

No, no. See, and we couldn't understand how we were paying more taxes and we were paying the same joining fees and whatnot, and we didn't have the same privileges. So it made us like second-class musicians, and we couldn't understand how you could have two locals in one jurisdiction in the same jurisdiction.
And these things would go on.
Well, the merging of the two locals in Chicago led then to a lot of other mergers.
Right, they merged all over the country.
That was during the civil rights movement, the heyday of the movement.
Right, yeah, right.
And then I thought it was quite ironic that, after Petrillo was defeated and he became president Emeritus of the International, --
Right.
-- and they made him head of the --
Civil rights of the Federation, the whole Federation. He was the chairman of the Civil Rights Committee. That was really an insult.
I remember writing a story for Downbeat, and we ran a picture of Petrillo, and the caption was "James C. Petrillo," -- and then the line under that was, "We shall overcome?" Question mark. (laughter)
Right, that was really a slap in the face, but nobody -- I mean, they got away with it.
Yeah. Well, Petrillo is still alive. Is Harry Gray still around?
He's still around. He wouldn't
accept a post in an integrated union.
Well, he was opposed to integrating the unions.
Yeah, he was opposed to integration.
Was that because -- I don't know, in your opinion, or do you know, it was because of money that he had coming, and by being president of this local, under the table stuff, or --
Well, --
Or was he really concerned about the investments of 208?

No, they couldn't have been, because the way they negotiated, they -- there was a lot of money missing, when they finally were going to merge. They were supposed to have turned over all the assets. They only turned over $38,000 in cash money. And then they had a building, so they turned this building over and $38,000. But they were talking figures of $250,000.
What happened to that money?
Well, this is what I'm saying. Now, there again, Price Waterhouse examined their books, 208, and come back with the conclusion that they couldn't give an accurate accounting.
So the Federation stepped in to save Local 208's face, and sent their auditor. And he gave them a clean bill

of goods. So that -- I mean, it goes to show you how these things have worked out from the higher-ups. And -- but they're doing it to protect each other, and they didn't want any -- they didn't want the waters to be ruffled at all.
In fact, a trustee of Local 10 for that period was Hal Davis.
Hal C. Davis, right.
He became president of International --
Of International.
-- and just recently died.
Yeah, recently died, right, right.
Yeah, I met him at that time, because we were covering the story.
Yeah, right, right.
And --

See, and at this time, I was an assistant to Barney Richards, and Leon Washington came in as a business agent, see, so that to be -- have some representation for the musicians who had come in before. Now, all of this is before the merger. See, this is before the merger. And so we were -- and then this is when the trusteeship and Hal Davis came in.
In fact, I came over to the union that day that you and the rest of the guys came in.
Right, right, right, right. I have
pictures and things of that, the news and the lawyers and all of that.
The union is something else. It has nothing at all to do with music, of course.
No.
But when did you first join the union? You had talked earlier about playing the Walkathons and the hustling gigs.
Yeah, right, right. Well, let's see, I think I first started joining the union when I -- in -- when I come to Chicago, here, in 193- -- yeah, about '33.
When you were through with the Walkathons.
Yeah, right, after I come back to Chicago, then I joined the union. Before, I didn't belong when we were hustling and things like that. Wasn't no cause, you know.
Well, did the union hassle you back in those days?

No, no, they didn't hassle. But if you wanted to work on the South Side, you would have had to be in the union. And when I say work on the South Side, they had boundaries at that time. This is before the merger or before anybody thought about the merger. They had boundaries. You couldn't work past -- black musicians couldn't work past 22nd
Street.
Yet some did, like Lee Collins, worked at the Victory Club.
This is not -- the point I'm talking about --
Oh, you're talking about the '20s.
Right, right, and the '30s, the early part of the '30s. But, see, I'm talking about the average -- I mean, any kind of a choice club, those were strip joints.
Yeah, well, Kelly's Stables --

Kelly's Stables had them for years. They had Johnny Dodds and Baby Dodds, and those people over there. But, I mean, they were just a few jobs, I mean, nothing like -- I'm talking about the hotels and no radio stations or nothing like that. And no regular bigtime jobs. Kelly's Stables considered a cabaret, a midnight, and that type of a thing, they let them do that.

But they had this boundary line. And then, at that time, they had a business agent by the name of Jaborotsky in 10. Great, big guy, boy, and he was rough. And he would come and he would go and threaten the proprietors and all of that type of a thing, get them out of here, and if I catch them in here, and he was liable to punch the musicians.
Oh, yeah, it was a -- well, people go into -- see, everything back in those days was muscle and force. Because
the joints were all owned by hoodlums and things like that. So it was a real rough deal for the musicians. But fortunately, as compared to today, --
(Recording interrupted.)
Comparing today with --
Yeah, right.
To those bad days.

Compared to today, the musicians on the South Side did have some clubs. They didn't play much money, but they had places to work, and today they don't have any places because of the disc jockey that come into the scene and he took the jobs away from them, and then the proprietor don't want -- after not paying musicians, you can't re-educate them to pay them now.

But back then, those days, they had all kinds of clubs, like the Delisa had a club and you had all kinds of taverns, and Swingland and all that. Just had a lot of places, all over the city, on the South Side, where you could work. And so the musicians were pretty much taken care of. But today it's a pitiful --
Well, Petrillo despite all his faults, did see the danger of records.
Yeah, right. When they had the strike back there, he fought that. And it was -- the disc jockey and the record industry has almost ruined the musician. They took
their own product and then just beat them across the head with it.
That's right. When did the night club disc jockeys come in on the South Side?
They have been in existence now about -- I would say, around -- in the early '60s.
Yeah, that's as I recall it.
Right, in the early --
I hadn't heard of that before.
No, no. But, see, what they would do is, when one guy is successful with one of the things, and monkey see, monkey does.
That's right.
So these guys would get a guy and pay him $30 or $35 for a night, and he'd play these things, and the latest records, and they're so loud you couldn't hear, and they --
The chatter...
Right, right, talking and all that. So it became a fad. And so, that's just shut the musicians completely out.
Yeah. Well, what about dancing? Back in the days when people went out to dance, wanted to go out dancing, there were always bands, --
Right, right, right.
-- for dancing, and then with the decline of dancing, and then with television coming in, --
Right, right.
-- and then these disc jockeys.
Right, right. Competely wiped them out.
Yeah. Is that ever going to change, do you wonder?

I don't know. We take old things, they never come back in the form that we once knew them. They may come back in different forms, just like they asked about the big bands. The big band today is almost an impossibility to run.
Now, they have big bands, -- Right, in the schools.

Right, in the schools and things like that, and -- but they're too expensive. Your salaries and the transportation is just almost -- and then hotels, everything that you -- food, everything, is so high, until it almost makes it impossible to operate.
Right. You've always been identified with big bands, I think, ever since the Delisa days.
Yeah, right.
Tell me something about your experiences with your own big band, at the Delisa and after-
wards, and some of the guys that were in it, and --
(Recording interrupted.)
Tell me something about the bands that you had, or did you just consider one band, or were there separate bands?
No, I mean, the bands wouldn't break up, but you just as well have said break up, because they -- the sizes fluctuated.
Was that because of economic conditions?
Well, yes, due to economic conditions. We started with a six-piece band.
At the Delisa.
Yeah, right, we started with a six-piece, and we kept that going for awhile, and then when we moved across the street in 1943, then we enlarged the band, see, we enlarged it to about 13 men.
Who were some of your key men?

Well, some of the key men, like Sonny Cohn, he's with Basie, I brought him in at that particular time, and then I had Earl Washington, well, he was a former brother-in-law of mine, and --on piano, and I had the boy now who's with the Trendiers, Walter Cole, he was on bass. And on saxes, we had Porter Kilbert. Did you ever know Porter?
I didn't know him, but I've heard him play.
He was one the great -- he used to work with Benny Carter, and he worked with Quincy Jones' band.
He worked a short while with Ellington, too.
Right, right.
He died in the early '60s.

Right, right, right. And so we had he and Harlan Floyd, Booby, he went with Basie, he worked with me, Johnnie Board. And it was just so many musicians that went through the band, and then Gene, Gene would come in and play with us occasionally, Gene Ammons. Yeah, he worked with us at times.

And then, -- well, all the musicians that we had, they'd come and they would go, for different reasons -- Army, different things. But we had quite a few musicians that as the years go by you kind of forget about them until you see them again. Right, and we had good trombones, Cy Touff, Dennis Farnan, you remember we was talking about Dennis Farnan, and Cy Touff, and Marty Martinez. I don't know whether you knew him, he was a Spanish guy, plays trombone very good.
So we always kept an -- but it didn't make any difference, because the club was an integrated club. So far as clientele was concerned.
Would guys come out and sit in?
Everybody.
And that's how you'd --
Right, right, see. We got to hear everybody, because that was the meeting place. And God bless the dead, when Sweet Pea --
Billy Strayhorn?

Billy, uh-huh, with Duke, he would make that his home. And then he'd get drunk we'd put him under the piano and let him sleep it off, because we'd be there til 5:00 the next morning. And Parker, Charlie Parker, he used to come out quite often, when he was in town, when he was working at the Rum Boogie. Yeah.
So -- Clark Terry, they were in the Navy at the time, and he used to come out, and they used to -- I don't know how those sailors did it. They were --
From the Great Lakes.
Great Lakes, they would take their leave and then get back just in time to go -- up all night long, yeah, really something.
Yeah. And there weren't very good roads, then.
On, no,no, no, right, right. That was really --
Had to be close to 60 miles.
Right, right, right, right. And then Hamp, and then on Tuesday nights we had celebrity night.
Oh, really?

Yeah, and on Tuesday night, I would -- I introduced it as celebrity night for them out there, and each Tuesday we'd invite whomever was in town, like, that time, Charlie Ventura when he had his little group.
(Inaudible.)
Yeah, oh, yeah, with Benny Green, and all of that.
Shelly Manne.

Yeah, and what's his name, Roy -- Kral. (Simultaneous discussion-- unintelligible.) Right, right, and then we'd have Louis Armstrong, and they'd come out and we could just turn the joint out. Boy, it was really something.
Yeah? Everybody played?
Everybody played. They just brought their horns and they just had a ball. And so -- and Stan Getz Gardner, Lionel Hampton, oh, it was just something else.
Yeah.
Right, and that was just like the meeting place of all the entertainers, because they would get off at 2:00. We were open until 4:00.
Well, that's an old South Side tradition, isn't it? Entertainers gathering in some place after hours on on or off nights.
Right, right. They have it right now, Von Freeman, he has his sessions out here.
I was just over to his house.
Oh, well, right, well, he has one, and there are ones that they go by and blow and have a ball on Monday nights.
Yeah, there are a lot of people that think Von is one of the great tenor saxophone --
Yeah, right, right, right, right.
Chicago is still a good breeding ground.

Oh, this is a good breeding ground, and this is a good town, if they'd just let it be itself, like, Chicago has always been known. Because when we take all of the greats that have come out of Chicago here, -- I got some articles I want you to look at I wrote for the Chicago Defender. And this goes back to the early '20s, and all of this. And you can see through that all the people who were centered right here (recording interrupted) Bill Robinson, END T1 S2 P2 and you would have all the horn players like Joe Oliver and -- were all here, and Louis Armstrong, Lil Armstrong and Erskine Tate. And that's an interesting man. Did you ever know Erskine Tate?
Well, I know the name. I've never met him.

Well, he was one of the great band leaders in the early '20s, and then at the Vendome Theatre he had this great band. And I guess back there -- I guess he had about 16 or 18 or 20 pieces, and they would play an overture and he had Jimmy Bertrand playing drums with him. He had Teddy Weatherford playing piano with him one time, then later he had Earl Hines playing with him, Louis Armstrong played with him. And Darnell -- everybody, Darnell Howard, all the guys, everybody. They played with him at one time here. And -- but what they would do, which is almost like what we're doing now, after they'd do this overture, then they would play -- well, they would have a whole concert. They would have a concert, say, about a half hour, and the pictures would go on. And a lot of times they would play the pictures.
This is at the Vendome.
Right, the Vendome.
Where was the Vendome?
The Vendome Theatre was on State Street, I think. Now, I'm trying to think whether it was in the 30 -- about 36th and State Street, on the -- yeah, right.
Well, you mentioned Jimmy Bertrand, who -- when I was learning to play, I got interested in the older forms of jazz.
Right.
I hear these records and Baby Dodds ---
Right.
I was fascinated by him. He seemed to be a very well rounded percussionist.
Oh, he was great.
In one round, there, he played the xylophone.

Oh, he was a great percussionist. He was a great -- see, this is what made the people take notice and the -- because this guy would feature -- each -- a certain guy in the band each week. And Jimmy Bertrand would either play his xylophones, with four mallets and things like that, and then he'd play tympanies and he'd play chimes.
And he'd also play washboard.
Right, right, he was with Jimmy Blyth on -- right, right, right.
You remember Jimmy Blyth?

Right, I remember. See, I was coming in -- I mean, I was coming in, and these guys were getting ready to go out, you know? And this was the thing. But I got a chance -- Jimmy Blyth was selling peanuts and popcorn at the Apollo Theatre on 47th Street. And they used to have -- they couldn't have a band, so they had piano players. And Jimmy Blyth used to play the pictures there. And then Tiny Parham played the pictures there.
So I got a chance to meet him and talk with him,

and then I used to listen to his records and all of that. But I was just the peanut and popcorn boy at that time. And then I would go and get a drum, it was just a snare drum, that's all I had, and then they would let me sit down there with them and play. Say, keep quiet, play quiet. No, that was my training grounds.
Sure.
With these guys, and they --
Did you hear Baby Dodds back in those days?
Oh, yeah, Baby and I were good friends.
You know, we were talking last week about the low hat and the high hat.
Yeah, right.
And you said, you said, back then, you can do anything if the left foot was free.
Right.
But Baby never did use --
He never used one the whole time.

I read an interview that somebody did with Baby that has not been published. A guy down in New Orleans has it. And Baby claims that when he was working the Streckfuss line, that Bill Slingerland or whatever his first name was -- this had to be in the early '20s.
Old Man Slingerland.
Old Man Slingerland.
Yeah, right, right.
Came on the boat one day and said his had this idea for this invention, and he took Baby's shoe size, and he came back later with a low hat (unintelligible).
Yeah, right, right, right.
And Baby said he didn't like it and never used it before.
Right, right.
But that he was -- it was his foot size.
Yeah, that must have been Bill Ludwig, Old Man Ludwig.
It was Ludwig --
Slingerland wasn't in -- yeah, right.
Yeah, the Old Man.
Old Man, right, they were always inventing something, they were very instrumental in a lot of new contraptions for drums.
I saw the Old Man play one time.
Did you?
With his son.
With Bill, Jr., right.
And they did a rudimental snare drum solo at a music convention.
Right, right.
At a music convention. The Old Man can still play that style.
Right, right, right, right, right.
You, of course, learned that traditional way of playing.
Right, right, right.
Yeah, I did, too. Didn't take me too long to figure out that they really weren't worth too much, except as exercises.
Right, exercises just to loosen up, that's about --
Yeah.
But Baby, he -- see, back then they didn't use the sock cymbal, like I said now. And they used the shimmy beat. And that's why --
Yeah, he was famous for that.
He was famous. A lot of fellows said that he -- who knows, said he invented it, but who knows?
What is the shimmy beat?
Shimmy beat is about a five-stroke roll.
On the afterbeat?
Yeah, on two and four. And it's -- and that's why Baby got that little shaking thing, and he could
shimmy, and see, he would shimmy, they'd call it that shimmy, so that's how they named it the shimmy beat.
Just a press roll.
Right, press roll, that's right, that's what it was, right.
Yeah.
And Zutty came along later, doing it. But (unintelligible), a drummer from New Orleans, started up-- they all played similarly.
Yeah, did you know many of the New Orleans musicians that were in Chicago?
Oh, yeah.
People from New Orleans were always pretty strange.
Yeah, right, well, see, I knew -- well, I worked with Guy Kelly.
The trumpet player.
Oh, man, he was a wonderful trumpet player.
Yeah, I have him some records with Jimmy Noon e.
Right, oh, yeah, right, right, right, right, right.
Natty Dominique was a --
And Natty Dominique and then -- but he
wasn't the musician that Guy Kelly and -- what's his name that just died down in New Orleans not too long ago?
Punch --

Punch Miller. Gee, I remember Punch when he was here, and we worked with Punch, and then Francois Mosely, I used to see him all the -- he had a band that called themselves the Louisianians. And he had a whole New Orleans band. Yeah. And almost all of the musicians from New Orleans -- we all mingled very close that year. So -- but they were very clannish, they stayed together. And they acted a little strange, like you said.
Zutty stopped talking to Louis or something because Zutty was the oldest -- this was later, of course, and Zutty was the oldest and therefore he had inherited the leadership or something.
Yeah.
They really --

Yeah, they have -- see, they have strange customs. If they adhere to them, they still have those same strange customs, like, on Mondays down there in New Orleans, if you go to the house, if a dark man comes in there first thing on a Monday morning, they won't let him in. If it's a light person, they let them in. So, I mean, one's bad luck and one's good luck.
So these are the type of things -- they still have
those superstitions.
And it's not just the black musicians. The white musicians --
Oh, yeah, they're all --
George Brunis was --
Yeah, right. Yeah, he was odd, right, right.
And even the younger musicians, like Wallace Davenport.
Right, right.
Wallace is --
Yeah, right, right. They all have their little queer things, right.
Yeah.
And we find it so different, and when I was down in New Orleans here in '68, I was at the first jazz festival they had. I went down with Art Hodes.
Right.
And so they had three bands on this boat. They had Sharky Bananas, then they had Peewee out of New York, and then Sharky was from New Orleans. And then our band from Chicago.
Peewee Russell?
Peewee Russell, right. And he had -- what's his name, playing bass with him, the --
Sharky?
No, no, Peewee, the band he had, the group out of --
Bob Haggart?

Bob Haggart, yeah, right, playing bass with him, and then Sharky Bananas had his band. So we went down there and we played on the boat, and whats' name, George Brunis was with us, yeah. But it was really amazing, to see these people bringing food, and I saw the biggest tambourine I've ever seen in my life -- about that big.
Really?
Right, about that big, man, --
So you're talking about 18 inches?
Right, yeah. And they would be -- that boat was rocking. They had over 2,000 people on there. The President was the name of the boat.
Yeah, I've been on it.
Right, have you? Right. And, boy, I'm telling you, they went out -- I mean, down the Mississippi there at night. It was a midnight to 11:00, 12:00 thing, and it was really something.
Yeah, that's a Streckfuss line. I think Streckfuss
Is that-- oh, yeah? Oh, yeah?
-- still in business. Yeah, it's one of the old boats. Big boat.
Right, right, right, big boat, right.
And New Orleans is such a -- you know, they talk about New Orleans style, and Chicago style. Do you believe there's a Chicago style of playing jazz?

Well, at one time there may -- at one time I think there was. But I think most of the jazz today is just like if you go to New Orleans, you find -- you can find the same kind of jazz you find in Chicago or New York or anywhere. But they stick to their tradition. But Chicago had -- not now --
I don't mean what is normally called Chicago jazz, like Jimmy McPartland and those guys. I don't mean that.
Oh, yeah, no.
I mean generally. Is there a different way of playing here than in other places?
I don't think so. I think not.
I think there is. The Chicago player plays harder.
Yeah.
More rhythmically, sometimes. I was talking to Quinn about this.
Uh-huh.
And he always remarks about the rhythmic drive of the Earl Hines band compared to other bands.
Right, right.
We got talking about this, and not ever young musicians, since I've been up here, that have -- there's a hotness or --
Right, there is a --
-- more drive.
Drive, and a more of a -- see, jazz, to the way I -- I mean, I --
I don't mean a particular style. I mean just an approach.
Oh, oh, you mean that way. Yeah, right, the approach is different, because --
That's what I mean.
Yeah, right. I think the reason for that is because they're hungrier.
Well, it's almost as though the city --

Right, that's it. That's what I said, it's a hard driving city, but New York is hard driving, was, at one time. But they had a little more, and then the guys here, they're more competitive among themselves. They don't say it, but they are. Right, they're more competitive, and this makes good music.
That's right.
Right, it usually makes good music.
But were there ever many cutting
contests around Chicago? I know there were in New York, and you were talking about them in Kansas City.
Right, right.
Was there very much of that in Chicago?

Well, we'd have it, but not to the extent of, like, Kansas City. They were obsessed with it. Because, I mean, if you lived in Kansas City you had to be the greatest in the world, you know. But, yeah, there were, a lot of them. They used to have these sessions here, and then over here on Monday mornings they used to have the jam sessions which would -- and that's what they really amounted to, was over there in the Pershing Hotel, there, in the bar there. They had that for years.
Yeah. When was this? This was in the '50s, the '40s?
This was in the '50s.
After the war.
Yeah, right. This was in the '50s and the early -- the first part of the '60s. And guys like -- this is where guys like Von Freeman and them cut their teeth.
Yeah.
Yeah, see.
Yeah, I remember when I first came to Chicago in the '60s, there were sessions every Monday night. Segal used to have sessions, and they'd present names --
Right, and this is why --
Johnny Griffin.
Right, Johnny Griffin and Gene Ammons.

This is why the influence -- I have a tenor player with me now, Lucious Washington, and everybody that hears him for the first time,they hear the influence of Jug in him. Because so many of the guys -- there's another guy around here named Prince James, I don't know whether you know him.
Yeah.
And he has that Jug influence.
E. Parker MacDougal

Right, right, yes, Jug. But, see, so I think that that kind of answers your question as to -- about Chicago's style, because if you have a style that come out of a town like that, you have so many guys who are influenced by him. And it just creates the thing for the whole city.
That's right. Yeah, well, the musician is going to be influenced, particularly in jazz.
Right, right. Generally by someone.

There's something else I've noticed about Chicago musicians, and I wondered if you agree with it, is that Chicago musicians, as you say, are competitive, but they're also accommodating, in the sense that -- say Dexter Gordon comes in.
Right.
And so there's Wilbur Campbell and maybe John Young.
Right, right.
Dan Shapiro in the rhythm section.
Yeah.
And the guys will play for the soloist rather than play for themselves.
Oh, right, right, right.
Which is good musicianship.
Right, right.
But you see that in other instances, in shows, for instance, when you play for shows. You see it in the symphony orchestra, of being able to interpret and play what's expected.

Right, there's a certain amount of pride in the musicians here. They -- the product, regardless of who's fronting it, the product has got to be good. This is the attitude that they -- and the thing that I think they strive for.
Right.
Right, uh-huh.
That's good.
That's very good, because it's just like you say, they play for the individual, don't care who it is, and so they don't go into this bag of starring themselves.
They can be very flexible.
Right, right.
And knowledgeable, too.
Right, right, right, right.
They can change what they might have done --
Before, right, and to fit within what he's doing.
That's right.

So this is why you find all of these guys who come in here and they augment with them, like Teddy Wilson and -- well, Dorothy or whoever it is, if he comes in town, and they augment with them, from local musicians. They're very, very satisfied. Marian McPartland, all of those, they're very, very, very satisfied with what they--
I was talking to Milt Jackson last week, went down to hear him a couple of times. I was so -- and so was he and everybody else -- Teddy Edwards, --
Yeah, right.
-- with the bass player and drummer, and particularly the drummer. I never saw Bags really turn around to somebody on the stand and tell him how to play, but he did then.
No kidding? Right, right.
And when I was leaving, I said, I'll
be back next week. He says, ah, Wilbur Campbell. I said, that's right.
(Laughter.)
Well, that's good, right, right. But, see, he's from that school of unity.
Right.
He worked all of those years with the Jazz Quartet.
[Modern]
Right.
And they were just like a glove on your hand. And so that's -- when you break into something like that, then other things kind of disturb you if you don't get it, yeah.
Right, but, he knew that there are better musicians available in Chicago that these guys from New York.
Right, right.
And it was unfortunate, because Barry Harris and Teddy Edwards and Bags --
Sure, right.
-- were a very interesting group.
But the rhythm section not very, but the bass player and drummer. Just drive me crazy.
Right.
Turning the time around, dragging
and -- oh, I mean, it was really amateurville.
Sure, sure, sure.
I told them, I said, I'll be back next week.
Yeah, right, right, right, right.
Tell me about some of your recordings, your own. When was your first recording?
Well, the first recording -- I can't remember when the first -- I made --
I mean as a sideman.

Well, as a sideman I made records with -- oh, I made -- we would go in the studio, like, with Big Joe Turner, and we would just play until he passed out. We'd make records. And then I made a lot of records for Decca, with Rosetta Tharpe.

And expose some of this --
Youth, the young talent, right. Well, you've got it, it's out here, you know?
That Governors State band is a killer.

Right, and, see, these -- you know, they get these band clinics in different places, like Triton College and all the different colleges they have, Notre Dame and all of that. You hear some fantastic music.
That's right.
Right.
Good soloists, too.
Right, right, right.
It used to be that the bands were very good, as far as reading their parts.
Right, right.
And the soloists were weak.
Right, right.
That's not true anymore.

No, no, it isn't true anymore. I mean, the level has improved, see, and by them getting the old masters and things and come in -- Kenton is great for that, doing these seminars in the schools, and Woody does them. All of the bands do that. And this exposed them to the real thing.
And it builds an audience.
Right, right.
With all these thousands of kids who not only have gone through the bands, but the other students who aren't musicians, who've heard the bands.
Right, right, sure.
I think that's part of the reason why jazz has a bigger audience.
Right, right. And -- but Maynard Ferguson, I mean, he's known as a school band, almost. This is where he really does his thing.
Oh, Woody and Maynard and Kenton also, draw their personnel right out of the schools.
Right out of the schools, right, right.
You've got to keep that payroll down.
Man, I -- right, right, right. I looked at that little young drummer with Woody -- was it Woody?
No, it was Basie.
Huh?
With Basie.
Not Basie, no. I know Butch, Butch Miles. I mean, --
He's something.
Oh, he's something else. He's --
I think he came through that college.
Did he? I'm not sure about him, but Woody had this little young drummer, man, and he was really saying something. Little bitty there looked like a -- I could spank him.
(Laughter.)
Right.
Yeah, there are some young --

Oh, yeah, they're really coming on and, see, they listen. They listen, and this is the only way you can really get a true picture of what's happening, is to be able to listen and to -- to the masters and improve themselves, see, and you listen to a improvement product, and this is how they develop.
That's right.
Uh-huh.
It really is amazing. You mentioned Bunky Green. Bunky's using a group of youngsters that were either his students or --
Right, right.
-- right out of school. Got a piano player, John Campbell, who really is something. Not many people know him. A young white kid. Looks like he's about 18 or something.
That's what I say. Some of them look so young.

Plays his ass off. You mentioned in your advice to young musicians, that they should -- if they're going to play reed instruments, they should learn to play all of the wind instruments and so forth. Did you follow your own advice and learn other percussion instruments?

Yeah, well, I learned, but I could only learn to a certain extent. I -- that was one of the things that I really hated. I studied vibes at the time, and then I studied a little tympani. But I had to get out and make a living, because my sister raised me, like I told you before. She was like my mother, and so when I went on the road, well, that just blew all the rest of my schooling and everything. So then the rest of it, you just had to be natural ability with -- and then I'd have to lean on what I had learned,
which I would have loved to have gone through and played vibes like you. You knocked me out when I heard you. Yeah, but, I mean, I just wished I could have studied more.
Did you ever run into some shows where you had to double tympany or --
Yeah, right, this is what I mean, seeing to certain parts and things like that. And I could do just enough of it to get the effect that was needed.
Yeah.

Right, and so -- but I would have liked to have been a virtuoso or whatever you want to call it on these instruments. Yeah. But after you get caught up in the business of making a living, and then playing and trying to get your -- raising a family and all of that, something has to give, and so your studying has to give, you give it up.
That's right. Now, you can learn a lot of things about playing jazz, in schools and -- but drummers particularly -- how do you learn what a beat is?
Yeah, you can't, you don't learn.
An old-fashioned beat.

Right, right, you've got -- no, no, no, right, that's right. And this is what I find that's lacking so much in most of the drummers that you run across today. They don't have that drive and that beat that you're talking about. They just don't have it. They're fooling
around with that left hand so much. And they don't give you that old back beat and that old sound that you want.
And the bass drum.
And the bass drum is another thing. They're playing tricks with it. Their feet are dancing, and they're trying to see how many taps they can make with it.
It's nothing like, say, a four-piece rhythm section in a big band, and the drummer playing the bass drum --
Right, right, right, right.
Get that round sound, lift the band up.
Sure. If it's not there, then you listen and you fill this emptiness.
No bottom.
Right, no bottom.
I heard Jo Jones lift the whole Basie band. This was right before it broke up and he went to the small band. And remnants of the original band, Harry Edison was still with him
Right, right.
Jo and Walter Page.
Right, right. That was a great bass player.
Yeah, they were playing a dance in
Louisville at this roller rink.
Oh, yeah, right, right.
And I don't know what Jo did. I've talked to him about this, but he did something with the bass drum, and -- played it louder or something. And, man, that whole band just went like that.

Right, well, when you talk about drums and things, drum -- Basie is a good example of that. I mean, his style, and he had to have that certain type of a drummer who shades. He shades. He can play, but he's very effective, but he's almost not heard at one time. This type -- and then if he wants to build, he's got the whole world to build on, because he can go to the limits. And so this is why they're so explosive, you would call it.
Yeah. And also, Basie's band, with Freddie Green, and whoever the bass player was.
Right.
They get that ball of sound. And the drummer has to really get in the middle of that ball.
Right, right, and this is the thing --
I never thought Sonny Payne did. I was not --
No, no. Well, he was a trick drummer.
Yeah.
His old man was a trick drummer, Chris
Columbus. But he was more or less a trick drummer and he looked good.
I mean, someone like Gus Johnson.
Right, right. Yeah, but, see, now, he reminds you of Sonny Greer in his day with Duke, with the flash and all of that.
So it came right down to beat, time.
Oh, beat, yeah, right, right.
Gus Johnson or Jo, when he was hot.
When he was hot, right, right.
And Sid Catlett.

Oh, yeah, he was -- well, see, we talked about that touch and that feel. Now, he had that shading type. And he could explode or he could play to a whisper. And this is what drumming really is all about. When you get in on that type of band. Because nothing stays at one level all the time. And then you have to have that type of a touch.

And this is why Basie is so hard. They have to really look around for -- when it comes to drummers, because, see, Freddy's not going anywhere. He's still there and he'll always be there, I guess, until he -- but they have to have that drummer that has that certain thing. And if he doesn't have it, he's not going to make it.
I heard them in --
The band won't make it.

No, no, the whole band won't make it. I heard them in Rotterdam. And they had a drummer out of Detroit. I don't know what his name was. And, oh, I've never heard the band sound so bad. Same men -- Lockjaw, what's his name, with his wa-wa, and all --
Al Grey.
Yeah, Al Grey and all of them. The same personnel, but that drummer changed the whole complexion. So they didn't keep him too long. Right after that they got Butch Miles.
Yeah, because in a big band, the drummer is really the heart.
Right, he's the heart. He can either make them or break them.
Who was it -- I think maybe it was if Jo Jones that said/the drummer doesn't feel good, the rest of the band is going to screw up.
Right, right, right, and that's true.
Why is that?

See, any drummer is not going to do it, though, see. It's got to be that certain -- it's a combination of things. I guess we could name four or five drummers that are playing in four or five different bands and the different bands have different styles. But they fit that

particular combination. So -- and -- but they've all got to have some type of rhythm. They can't be jumping around on the instrument, and then running all over the instrument. See, it's just not effective. It's not effective.

Well, is there, in your opinion, and of course, you're one of the most experienced big band drummers, is there a secret to big band drumming? Do you play on top of the beat, behind the beat? I've heard guys say both ways. But what is big band drumming and how does it differ from combo drumming, in your opinion?

Well, big band drumming, I mean, with the big bands, see, you've got different sections. You've got your brass section, your trumpets, your trombones and then you've got your reed section there, you've got your rhythm section and all that. Somewhere over this whole thing, you have got to fit in there, you've got to fill up holes. But you've got to know when to fill those holes. Then you've still got to carry that beat, carry that -- make the band move, whereas with the small combination, you're playing very light, maybe a lot of brushes and a lot of things like that. Brushes are very effective, only it's limited in a big band, because the main thing of it is, you have to keep that band together. And then, this is the -- that's the most important thing, and this is a function of a drummer in a big band. And then, when you can get one that's able to fill up

the holes and look good and do this, then he's very flashy and then he looks good in the group, but yet he's doing -- Butch does that, Butch Miles, with Basie, he does that. He looks real good, but -- I think when he first joined the band and from the time he joined the band up until this time, I think he's had a lot of instructions and a lot of tips and different things from the guys in the band and all of that, as to how he supposed to play in the band.
See, he joined them from Mel Torme and this is where he come from when --
I didn't know that.

Yeah, he had been with Mel Torme and this is where they got him from. And, see, usually they play with trios and things like that. So this is the secret of that, the band, the big band drummer. He's got to take command. He's the general, really, he's the general. And he can be soft as cotton, playing soft as cotton -- what did they use to say, he's so soft you could hear a chinch piss on a cotton.
(Laughter.)
But then the next minute, he flows, and this is really what makes a big band drummer.
Yeah, well, it wasn't always that way. In the earlier days, say, in the '30s, the rhythm section was more of a section and just sort of kept the pulse.
MR. SAUNDERS: Right.
How did that change? Now, the drummers catch brass licks and thing like that.
Right, well, --
When did that start coming in?

Well, all of this started coming in, I guess, maybe you could say from the time of the Chick Webb band into the Benny Goodman band and things like that. I think it's that late that this would come in. See, and the reason that is, is because the arrangements changed. And the arrangers changed, and the arrangers wanted certain effects and things like that.
And then all of these licks, they wanted these licks heard -- I mean, accentuated.
Yeah.
In other words, it was a brass lick, they wanted it accentuated. And to really accentuate it, the drums would come in with it. Yeah, see, they would do that. That's how that --
So you say around the early '40s?
Yeah, right, well, in --
In the '40s;
Yeah, right, right, right, right, right.
Well, how --
Late '30s, you know.
How did you play, if you can recall, when you first started playing for the big band?

See, I was a combination drummer. I did the shows, and then I had to do one thing with them, and then it made it easier for me playing in the big bands, because with the dances and all these type things, you caught the little cute things that they were doing, and different things like that.
So then it just spills over into the band. And when you do that, then you get the little cute things that they're playing in the horns.
That makes sense.
Right, uh-huh, right.
So you always were catching things in the band?
Yeah, right, right, right. Yeah.
That was -- you were one of the first to do that, I guess.
Well, it was -- well, Sid would do those things. Big Sid would do those things.
With Louis' band.
With Louis' band and things like that, because he was -- and then he played with Benny's band.
Right.

And things like that. And he was doing all of those things then. Because he was -- they would call them cute drummers, at that time. He's a cute drummer, he's playing them little cute things. Right, then later Jo came along and he was doing it.
Right. Well, he started using some accents with the bass drum.
Yeah, right, right, right.
Freed it up a little bit. You mentioned Sid Catlett. Oh, yes, did you ever hear a drummer named Coltsville Harris?
I heard --
Worked with Louis.
Yeah, I heard thename, but I never, never met him.
He's one of my boyhood heroes.
Oh, no kidding?
Used to hear Louis' big band when I was in Louisville.
Right, right.
And he was a drummer.
Uh-huh.
Very much like Sid Catlett. He'd get that dark sound.
Right, right, right, right.
And -- but very few people have heard of him.
Right, I --
He used to wear this big white towel around his --
I heard of him. Back there there was some real -- Jesse Price was another out of Kansas City. I don't know whether you ever heard of him or not.
Oh, yes, on records.
Oh, oh, yeah, right. Jesse was a real nice guy, and then Louis -- I mean, with Louis, when he was with Lu Russell's band, they had Paul Barbarin.
Right, he was from New Orleans.
Right, New Orleans type drummer. So this is what I was talking, when I was saying about different flavors. And it was a different flavor all together with that band than with Big Sid Catlett.
Well, when did guys start playing ride cymbals?
Well, like I told you earlier, we talked about it. Now, in 1932, that was -- there was a lowboy, see, and right after that, I would say, between 1932 and 1935, they started coming out with --
I don't mean the high hat, but, I mean, a top cymbal and riding --
Oh, riding, oh. Well, they've been doing that a long time.
Did you ever hear of Walter Johnson?
Walter Johnson, right, right.
He's the first one I heard to play the high hat.
Yeah, right, well, see, that was quite a few years ago.
Right, right, right, right, right, right, right.
And I guess around then the guys started playing the high hat, too.
Right, right.
Before that, it was mostly the snare drum.

Right. Well, like, see, we explained earlier, that was that shimmy beat thing we used to talk about, that five-stroke roll. And Baby Dodds and Zutty Singleton, all that come out of the New Orleans type of drumming.
Krupa was playing that way for Benny Goodman.
Right, right, he certainly was.
He didn't play the ride cymbal.
No, no, no. Right, right, right.

Well, see, Krupa, when they were here in the early days, like when that Austin group and all that was going, and the Midway Gardens was going there at 60th and Cottage Grove. And all those -- but, see, guys like Baby Dodds and all those -- he was around them a lot. And so a lot of that wore off.
There was another good drummer that I liked. Of course, I just heard him on records. Johnny Wells.
Yeah, Wells. See, he worked with Jimmy Noone Yeah, Johnny Wells was --
JOHN Wells.
Johnny Wells, right, right. He was a very, very good drummer. But it was a small group thing. Jimmy Noone was making all of those things, Sweet Lorraine and all of those things.
EARL Hines' band?
Yeah, right, right.
The drumming on there is --
Oh, yeah, right.
Is different from drumming on other records that were coming out then. I know Krupa has talked about Johnny Wells.
Right, right. Well, see, they had a-- when they were working at the Apex Theatre, Earl Hines, Johnny Wells, I think, and --
Joe Posten.
Joe Posten and Jimmy and --
Bud Scott?
Bud Scott on banjo, right. Right, right, right, and see, they were playing all of the things. And they were right across the street from the Sunset.
Where was that?
That was at 35th Street.
35th and Calumet?

And Calumet, right, see, and the Sunset was there across the street. Yeah. So music has been -- in Chicago -- but it was exposed more because the people -- I don't know, maybe the people that migrated here from New Orleans still had that New Orleans feeling because they love music down there, and they loved it out here, then. But since that time, I mean, people -- it's good music, but it's very -- you've got to go and find it.
Yeah, because it's more different kinds of music.
Right, right, right. And then people have started to choosing, and this is avant garde and this is swing and this is Dixieland and so it's all divided up, the whole thing is.
Yeah, and that's to be expected with human beings, but it's unfortunate as far as music is concerned because --
Oh, right, right. If we could change, right.
Right, and it divides people.
Right, right, right, right.
Now, tell me about drums. How have drums themselves changed over the years? Of course, the heads changed.
Yeah, the heads changed from the cowhide and then they went into the plastic and all of that, and then years ago they had a rope across and you pulled this --
Yeah, that's a long time ago.
Right.
Leather tong.
Right, right.
But I mean modern drums, with --

Yeah, right, right, well, the 1 s and things have changed. And then they've added -- like, it used to be that you used one tom-tom, and a floor tom-tom and one on top. And now you got to use -- it's nothing to see a guy with ten tom-toms.
Yeah, that's true. That came in with the rock group.
Right, right. So --
(Inaudible.)
And then they got -- they used to have

a couple of cymbals or whatever and now there may be five, six cymbals up there. And then there are two bass drums that come into the thing, into the scene and so a drummer is really -- he's really got to decide which way he wants to go now, because -- whether he's going to use two bass drums and sacrifice the sock cymbal or one bass drum. I mean, it throws them into a kind of a dilemma.
Well, what is your drum setup?
My drum setup is just two tom-toms, one on top (inaudible).
Do you use a large floor tom-tom or the smaller --
I got a big tom-tom there. I use a big sized tom-tom. And then the two cymbals.
You just use two top cymbals.
Two top cymbals, right.
What sizes are they?
Well, one is about 13 thin, and --
You use that for splash and crash?
Right, right, right. And then I got about a 18 on top, my heavy cymbal.
(Recording interrupted.)
Cymbals seem to have grown.
Yeah, they were growing -- well, back in '34 --
Cymbals seem to have grown.
Right, well, that was about the biggest thing you could get at that time. And then they used to have those old thick cymbals, so thick until -- they were almost like a gong.
Yeah, we used to call them brass cymbals because (inaudible).
Right, right, right.
With the big cuff.
Yeah, right, right.
I used to use that on the bottom of a high hat when I first started.
Yeah, right, right, I did, too, I did, too, and then have a thin one on top.
Right.
What about sticks? Sticks used to be heavier, it seems.

Yeah, I started out with heavier sticks, and I always compared a drummer with an athlete, with his feet and his legs and arms, muscles and all of this type of thing. As you grow older, you use a much lighter stick because you can't handle that heavy stick anymore, you know. Your wrist, your muscles and things just won't let you do it.
Yeah. I saw a young drummer here a few months ago, in town, a young rock drummer, and he looked
like he was using those oldtime practice sticks.
Yeah, right, yeah, right, right, right and then sometimes, they turn them around and use the butt end, and that's even bigger.
Right. It affects the sounds you get, there's no doubt about that, the weight of the stick.
Oh, right, right, right.
And certainly, playing shows, whenever I played shows, I'd have to do a lot of rolling, I like a heavier stick, because it's easier to roll.
Right, right, they are, right, right, right.
Do you use an open or a closed roll?

I use a more or less an open roll. I don't use the closed so much, unless I'm going to do something like a solo or something like that, and then I want to close it up and then I want to open it up, or something like that. I do it like that.
But, basically, I use an open roll, a lot.
(Inaudible.)
Yeah, right.
That -- somebody said -- Buddy Rich, that the best way to practice is just practice a roll, nothing but roll for an hour or two build control in the wrists.
But it'll do that. It's according to

what kind of a roll you're going to do. Right, right. But that is good, because it's in the wrists. You get your wrists supple and everything, and once they're there, relaxed and everything, well, you can do almost anything you want to do.
Yeah, once you get that good, warm feeling in your hands.

Right, right, right, right, right. I was explaining to somebody the other -- not too long ago, they was asking me about the same subject we were talking about on the drums and things, and I said, well, basically the whole secret of it is in your wrists. Because they can tie your arms down and just leave your hands and your wrists open and you can play all the drums you want. You don't have to go up in the air with your sticks and all of that, but you get the same effects that you want with them.
That reminds me of something. Guys that always used to throw the sticks up in the air.
Right, right, right.
When did that start?

Well, that started years ago. It was -- that was called showmanship. And in 1933, I worked with a show, and this act had been on RKO and it was one of the biggest acts in the country, called Norman Thomas' Quintet. And they had this little drummer they called Rastus, and he was about -- oh, I guess he was about four-something feet, and

weighed about 85 pounds. Real, real little bitty guy, but, oh, was he agile. And he would take the sticks and he would juggle them, do four and five -- you know they used to have the thing where they'd put them on the ground.
I've seen Hamp.

Right, Hamp does it, right. Five, six sticks and throwing them up in the air and all of this, and he would be doing that. And then they had a finale in the act, and he would -- see, the drummer in the pit would have to keep the time going, because he was just a trick drummer and he would jump up and hit the cymbals and all, and jump up in the chair and up and down and all of this kind of thing. And then he would run to the edge of the stage and run all across the stage, and then slide.

And they had a pit -- I mean, at the end of the pit there, he had a cymbal and he would hit the cymbal and it was right over the head of the pit drummer. And one day he hit some powder or something on the stage and he went right down into the drums.
(Laughter.)

Yeah, so -- but he was one of the trick drummers. And then they had Jack Powell. I don't -- do you remember him? And they called it his Musical Kitchen. And he was a drummer, and he had all of the pots and the pans and all of this type of thing. He was a white drummer, tremendous. Jack Powell.
This was all on the vaudeville circuit, during the vaudeville days. And he -- I caught him a lot of times.
Well, I guess it was because of things like that and, as much as I loved him, Gene Krupa, too, that --
Yeah, he had that flair.
-- that made it very difficult for musicians, or drummers to be accepted as a musician.
Right, right, right, right.
There are still guys that do that.
Oh, yeah, right, right, right.
A fairly young drummer around town, Johnny Faren, --
Oh, yeah.
-- who does all that crap. He goes out on the floor and plays on the floor --
Plays -- right, See, that was the thing then.
Saw him one time, he made me so mad. I was thinking about all the cats that don't do that and refuse to it, and trying --
Right, overcome that image.
(Unintelligible) seven piece band, wants six musicians and a drummer.
Right, yeah.
That is still with us.
Yeah, right, oh, yeah, right.
Particularly on horn players.
Yeah, right, right.
Don't have the proper respect.
Uh-huh, that's true, too, right.

But that was the thing, now, what they used to do. And the big thing back in the late '20s and early '30s was the Tiger Rag. That was a great tune. And then the drummer, he would have to see that the bass player would make that (sound) with his bass horn. They were doing the bass horns then. And then the drummer, if he didn't have the bass, then the drummer would take his snare drum off and blow into the snare side, (sound) and you'd get that sound from there.
Yeah.

And that was the sound from there, from the Tiger Rag. And then the drummer would get ready for his solo and he'd run all over the place and play on the tables and chairs and all. But this is -- they call that getting hot.
Well, I always delighted in the story of Kaiser Marshall --
Yeah.
-- that was with Henderson. They were playing a dance, and he tossed a stick up and never
bother about catching it. He'd pick up another one.
(Laughter.)
That sort of thing really has hurt the art of drumming and it's hurt drummers being --

Well, it would have been all right if they had elected -- see, in the era they were coming up, this was the Roaring Twenties and all of that type of thing and all that, and there were so many things that were accepted then, and expected then. Like, a black band was the hot band. They had to play the hot music, and maybe they'd have another band over here playing the sweet things and the soft things, and then a hot band. And so, to get hot they had to do a little bit of everything -- visual and playing.
That carries over. I know a lot of people go to hear a combo or a big band, and they go there to watch the drummer.
Oh, yeah, right, right.
They don't go there to watch --

Oh, no, but, see, that's showmanship. But, really, today the people are more musical conscious. They like to hear these beautiful arrangements, they like to hear these beautiful -- I mean, the exact sounds and great soloists and all of this type of a thing. And it has taken away from that period. You don't need that now, no.
So now -- and this is the thing, when you're

listening to a band, I mean, you hear the big band in concert, you don't hardly hear drum solos hardly, too much, even here. I mean, extended drum solos. You may hear eight bars or something like that, or 16, but that's about it. You don't hear a lot of drum solos, that much.
Well, I've found that horn men, I had to train them that I played with -- if I was going to take a solo on something, 32-bar tune, that I would play choruses.
Right. Right, right, 32 bars --
(Unintelligible.)
No, no, no, no, no.
Because drummers are --

In your mind, you're hearing the sound of a tune. I'll tell you, what you're saying was when Sonny Payne would take his solo with Basie that time, and they would do that 'Old Man River.' Now, he would do the rolling, but he would roll practically through the whole solo. But it was through the rhythmetic pattern of the whole tune. You could follow up 'Old Man River.'
You heard the changes.
Right, right, right.
Where I learned that was listening to Sid Catlett.
Right, right, right.
Sid was the most melodic drummer I've ever heard.
Right, right, right, right.
He played little tunes.
Right.

And, again, this is what I was talking about earlier. The drummer being accepted as a musician by the other musicians, like, drum soloists, there's a time to talk and there's a time to get off the stand and have a drink.
Right, get off the stand and have a drink, right, no, no, right, right.
And I had to train some very experienced musicians.
Yeah, right, right.
Don't do that.
Just to undertake three chorus es or whatever, right.
Right, and come back in, and don't come back in --
Right, right.
You either (unintelligible) change keys when you came back in and then tell me you're going to change keys.
Right, right.
That would throw me (unintelligible).
Right, right, right, right, right.
But it's -- I'm sure all drummers have felt this, that they're not comedians.

Right. Well, that's true, too, that's true. But, see, it's just like anything else. It's just a thing that happened years ago that you have to live down, and you're not going to live it down in two or three days. It's going to take time, a lot of time, for it to live down.
That's why it's good to see somebody like Louie Bellson, who likes beautiful arrangements, too.
Right, right.
But they're looked upon as exceptions. That's one reason I took up vibes. To try to overcome that.
Yeah.
That's a very sore point with me.

Right, right. Well, see, where your musical knowledge is extended, you would be more offensive than another guy with less musical ability. He -- maybe he wouldn't even pick up on that particular point. So -- and then Basie and them, they was -- on bad nights he'd let everybody go home. And so --
That's right, they came up here in the winter.

Right, and do they would come over and they would come to the breakfast shows and all of that. And then this is when I really met and got close with Jo Jones, because Jo -- I don't know, he took a liking to me and he used to come around all the time. So did Sid, the last days, when he -- well, we had been friends down through the years, but not where he was always like in New York or somewhere like that. And then the last years -- I mean, the last year or two, he was here at the -- with Bill Rinehart at the Jazz Limited.
And we were really close then. And he lived in one of my sister's buildings. He had a room there.
Where did he live?

63rd and Ingleside. So he was living over there. And then, the day that he dropped dead was on a Easter Sunday, I think it was either '51 or '52, at a concert by Al Benson. And I told you the story about keeping the Easter egg from him. So -- see, this is the thing that's so wonderful, is all of these beautiful stories, and they crop up every now and then in your mind, and you think about this different person and that -- Louis Armstrong, and you can think about --
Pleasant memories.
Pleasant memories of all these different people.
All great people, too.
Yeah, right. Well, not only great musicians, but -- it's like I was telling you about Fats. I mean, he was more of a character offstage than he was on-stage.
Dizzy's that way, too.
Dizzy is a very, very --
A natural comedian.
Right, right, right, very comical.
Well, to go back to Basie, how did your friendship with Basie develop? Just from seeing each other, or --
No, in Kansas City, I mean, --
No, after that.

Well, after that it was periodic. And then the thing about it, he would steal my men, and I'd get mad as hell, yeah. And when he took Sonny Cohn, that was the thing. That was my first trumpet player. I almost died. But then he'd say, that's all right, I'll send you some arrangements.
(Laughter.)

So -- and then, as the years go by, then I visit with him every time I get a chance, to catch up. Then the Joe Williams incident, Joe Williams was with me, I was managing him at that particular time. And then he left me and went with the Count Small group.
Yeah, the Count Small group was playing down on Randolph.
Randolph Street, right, at the Brass Rail.
The Brass Rail.
Right. And then he was there, and then we used to --
I didn't know that Joe worked with him at that point.
Yeah, right.
And then Basie had put the big band --
And then the big band, and then Joe --
But he had worked with a small band.
With a small group, right. Clark Terry was in the group.
Yeah, Buddy DeFranco.
Yeah, right, right, right.
I'd like to hear them. They made one record, but I've never --
They didn't do too much recording.
They just took one album for Norman Granz, but I've never heard it, and it's very rare.
Yeah.
So he's going to be at your 50th anniversary.
Yeah, he's going to be at the 50th anniversary, and no problem of getting him at all. He was only too happy. I talked with Sonny, the musical director. He takes care of most all of the business.
Sonny Cohn does.
Yeah. So they're going to play with Billy Eckstein sometime this month or the first of next month, anyway, for four days. So he told me, don't have to worry about a rehearsal. That's $400.
Sure.
See, so you don't have to worry with
the rehearsal. We'll save you that amount of money. So it's like that type of a feeling.
Do you expect anyone else to come on?
Well, I'm looking for Louis because he's going to be in town.
Louis -- ?
Louis Belson. Yeah, I got --
He's a beautiful man.
Yeah, and then I talked to Cozy Cole a couple of days ago, and he's down in Columbus -- he lives in Columbus, Ohio now.
He does? He moved from New York?
Right, he moved from New York. He's left Jonah Jones, and he's living -- and he's free lancing. He's going to school in the University of Ohio, going to school and studying arranging.
Cozy is?
Cozy Cole, and --
Isn't that amazing?
So great, and he wanted to be here so bad, but he's going to be in Europe.
It's like when Kansas Fields came in the other day, --
Right.
And he told me he was going to State.
Right, right, right, right.
Studying music.
Right, right. Cozy wants to arrange, so he's taking theory and all the harmony and all that now.
He -- when you were talking about drumming earlier, he changed his grip a few years back to the mash grip, tympany grip.
I didn't notice. I saw him not too long ago, but --
And I think it affected his playing.
Yeah, I didn't --
He doesn't play as well.
No, he doesn't, no, he doesn't, no. He does better with his hands. He does that thing with his hands, you know what I mean?
Cozy was one of the great drummers.
Oh, yeah, he was very, very --
Strong.
Right, right, right.
Almost like a metronome.
Right, he was, right, right, right. But he's -- well, that's what's happening to him now. And he was so glad when I called him. I called him to say Hi and I
wanted to let him know about my 50th anniversary, if he could make it.
Well, where did you meet Cozy?
Oh, I met Cozy from the Cab Calloway days. Yeah, when he and Jonah -- I knew Jonah --
I saw him with Cab.
Did you?
That was when Little Joe was popular.
Yeah, and then --
This little kid.
Right, right, right, right. Then I knew him a little before that, because I knew him from the Stuff Smith days.
Ah, yeah.

He and Jonah, right. He and Jonah were in it, see, and that was the band and they used to go -- oh, they used to go crazy, they'd go nuts. What's his name that played here, one of the first black bands to play in the LaSalle Hotel, which is gone now. But they played an engagement down there, and Stuff was there. And Stuff was crazy, he was really a nut. And he had these guys -- he'd see a woman, he'd say I'm going to go over there and kiss her. And he would do it.
(Inaudible.)
Oh, right, right, right. I had some great times with him. And then he -- you talk about Jo Jones being a nut, there's another one. That was his brother, Stuff Smith.
Ehenezek.
Yeah, right. Ezekiah.
Ezekiah. And he's like Joe, he's got all those names.
Yeah, right, right, right, right.
Well, you've heard Joe recite his name s la-la-bla-la-la.
Right, right.
Well, the Kirby band played around Chicago.

Yeah, Kirby, and then -- see, I had a combination, well, six pieces, like he did. And we just took the tenor player and let him play the clarinet part, and then the alto. And Kirby gave us a lot of opus, 'Opus One' and all of that thing.
Right, 'Dawn on the Desert.'
'Dawn on the Desert,' all of those things.
All the strippers use that.
Right, yeah.
'Twilight', that was Raymond
Scott.
Raymond Scott, right, right. But he gave me some of those arrangements.
Do you still have that stuff?
Yeah, I think I've still got some over to my ex-wife's house. I got a whole batch of music from that era.
Really?
Right. And I have never really gone through it. But I'm sure I can find some of those Kirby arrangements and all that stuff.
Be interesting to --
Right, right, right, because it's just like they did them.
I know the Institute wants to establish an archive here, for historical documents.
Well, that would be beautiful. Well, those things, I would only too happy to, because, like, the Institute and the museum -- what do call it, the New Orleans --
New Orleans Jazz Museum?

Jazz Museum and stuff, when we were with Art Hodes, down there, I put a pair of sticks in there. But I would like to -- I go through this music, or we could get somebody to go with me through it, because I have the book from the old Delisa and all those things, and we could go through there

and maybe we could pick out some things. Because every once in a while, man, if I really want to get nostalgic, I go there and look through this music, man, and this music brings back all of the things.
Did he always write drummer parts for you?
With me? They -- a lot of times, on account of conducting and leading the band and all of that, I had more or less a guide. Like, what I would do, --
A cue sheet.

Yeah, a cue sheet. Whatever the introduction was, if I had to write up a four-bar introduction, I would do that. Then I'd write so many choruses, four choruses, so-and-so, eight bar tag, so-and-so, this type of a thing. And this gave me the freedom of playing, unless it was an act that required you to read the part, because I know once I had to play a thing for one of the rock and roll singers at the Regal. And there was a tune, and I had to read this thing, because of the way that the licks and things were to be, and it was all synchronized right with the arrangements and had to be that way. Yeah.

This brings up another point about the drummer as musician and the attitude of musicians toward a drummer as being not quite a musician like they are. It is that -- they'll write arrangement for a band, and if they write
No, no, no.
And it's like sort of a non-instrument to them.
Right, right, right. A lot of guys really -- yeah, but a lot of them really don't know how to write, like you say. They really don't know how to write.
Well, they have to study the instrument.

Right, right, right, yeah. I tell you now, who has been instrumental in creating a lot of things like drummers is a man named Bill Ludwig, I mean, the old man, and then the son came along, and they were very instrumental. I mean, they stayed right on -- because they were one of the first drum companies, Ludwig and Ludwig. Yeah, and whenever anything new would come out, they would --
Yeah, they've always been quite innovating. Talking about music, going around in circles and things coming back, and the same thing with drums. Now, the big thing is wood drums, with which we're --
Right, and size. First they down to nothing, --
(Inaudible.)
Right, right, right.
Right.
Right.
That's funny. Do you still use a big bass drum with your band?
Yeah, my bass drum is -- I got a -- well, it's not a 28, I think it's 26, yeah, 26. I got a 26. But I was down to a 20 at one time.
That's not big enough for a big --
No, no, no, no, no, no, no. It's just not --
Doesn't have that resonance.
No, no, no, it's too thin. You don't get that boom.
Right, and beater balls, that's a different sound.
Right, right, right.

I've got an old sheepskin that I use for certain things. Well, there's a band that I'm rehearsing with tonight, a small band, but a mid-'30s band, what we're trying to do. And I think I'll take my sheepskin beater ball.
Yeah, right, right.
To get that --
You get a round sound, you get the correct -- you don't get that bop bop with that hard mallet.
That's right.
Right, see, and that was what they
A lot of sound -- guys try to create the sound of the '20s or the '30s, but a lot of that was in the instruments that were used.
Oh, yeah, right, right.
I'd love to get an old vibraphone.
Oh, right, right, right.
to do quartet stuff.
Yeah, right.
It was a different sound. Same way with the drums.
Right, right, right.
I imagine the horns, too.
Yeah, right.
Nobody's ever gone in to how the development of musical instruments has affected the music.
No, no.
For instance, there would be no rock and roll without the development of the Fender bass.
The Fender bass, right.
That's the basis of it all.
Right, that is right.
You couldn't do that on an a-coustic.
No, no.
So that changed the course of music.
Right, right, right.
Well, it's a subject that maybe we shouldn't be talking about, but an interesting one. You mentioned Rosetta Tharp last week, that you worked some with Sister Rosetta Tharp.

Yeah, I -- Bobby Shad was with Decca at that particular time. And we would go in the studio, he would go in the studio, and it was nothing for us to record 15 sides or 16 sides in a day, one right after the other. They'd just get the chord changes and then they would go ahead and do them.
Yeah.

Yeah, right. And I had -- well, like, gospel music. I did, on Channel 26 here, they had a gospel show -- and Gate mouth Moore. I don't know, do you remember him? He was a blues singer at one time, then he turned to be a minister.

So he had this show, and he would bring all of these gospel people in, and the union required them to have one union musician, so I was the musician. And then they brought their own organ player and piano player and I'd have to get the length of the tunes and all that straightened out with them and everything.
And I played with a lot of them. That's a strange
feeling, too, because they get in some terrible grooves.
That's right.
Right, right.
Did you ever know Loveie Austin?
Loveie? No, I didn't know Loveie too well, because Loveie was --
A little before your time.
A little before my time, and then she was a rehearsal piano player around here for -- I think it was Sammy Dyer, one of them.
The choreographer.
Right, and then she in later years -- this is how she made her living, doing the rehearsals for that, and then the dancing classes and all of this type thing. Right.
But you did know Lil.
Oh, I knew Lil, right, right.
Ever since you were a child.
Right, ever since I was a child. She used to put diapers on me and she used to tell everybody, 'boy, I used to put diapers on you.'
(Unintelligible.)
Right.
But she knew --
This was in Memphis, see, this was

what she meant, right. Yeah, she was a grand woman, and then I went up to -- at a country place up in Idlewild, Michigan. And whenever I felt depressed or wanted to get away from it all, I'd run up there -- it's in the summer, and she'd cook and all of that.
Was she a good cook?
Oh, tremendous, man.
(Unintelligible.)
Right, right, so she -- and she'd cook and everything and she loved that man til the day she died.
I know it was a very interesting relationship because she's good friends with Lucille.

Oh, yeah, she's a good -- right, right, she was a great friend of Lucille's, but she still -- and she always talked about Louis and their association and their marriage and all of this, and Louis just could do no wrong. And then whenever he would come -- like he was here at Revenue one year, and so she went up and she just a ball with him. Oh, Pops, you're crazy.
That was an interesting relationship.
Right, and then until the day she died -- and then, this home up there -- she was going to will that to Louis, but he passed just before her.
Just a month or two before.
Right, but she was going -- that country -- because she said, he bought this for me, so I'm going to give it back to him.
Well, she lived in the house that they had on --
There on 44th Street.
On 44th Street.
Right, right, right.
All her life.

All her life, right. I used to love to go down and hear her playing, and then she'd sing a lot of -- she went to France and she stayed over there -- oh, I don't know, for years, and she fell in love with Paris.
That's easy to do.
And then she learned to speak French fluently. And then she would come down and --
I didn't know that.
Oh, yeah. And then when she was -- just before she passed, she was teaching French at classes. She was teaching.
I didn't know that.

Yeah, and then she'd play those songs, 'Pardon, Pardon,' and she'd play all of these songs from France, and then she played a lot of her original things. She never did get credit for 'Strutting with Barbecue' and --
Well, they just had L. Armstrong, but it was Lil.

Lil Armstrong. See, she used to write -- see, Louis at that particular time was just more or less an ear type musician. She taught him how to read and things like that. She taught him a lot of things. And -- but she was the one that was really writing the tunes, and then when they would go into the studios, well, they would change the names on them. You know how the record business has always been shady like that.

So she would do it, and her 'Strutting with Some Barbecue,' and so many things that she wrote. And then this other thing, she used to do a tune called 'Clip Joint,' and I used to love to hear her -- every time, I'd say, 'Lil, sing Clip Joint for me.' That was one of my favorites.
Well, I always felt that she was the reason for Louis' success, in urging him to leave Oliver and go with Henderson.
Right, right.
And then lining up all this work for him, getting back here and I would imagine that she had line up the OK recording contract for the Hot Five before --
Right, well, she was a great business-woman because, see, she had her band in the Dreamland Cafe, and then she and -- because, see, at that time, he was working
with Erskine Tate, too, at the Vendome.
Right.

And so she had him to come over -- after he would finish there he would come over and work with her. And then this is how the association -- and finally they got married. Started going together -- but that was her band. He was working in her band then.
Yeah.
And then later on, in later years, he got the Hot Five, and then she --
Well, the Hot Five, the first records were made soon after he came back to Chicago to work --
Fletcher.
After he left Fletcher and came to work with Lil at the Dreamland.
Right, right.
Then within a month they made the first Hot Five record.
Right, right.
Richard M. Jones was (inaudible).
Yeah, right, right.
But I've always thought that Lil must have lined that all up.
Lil was so instrumental in Louis' success, more so that people would really realize. Because

she'd talk -- he was just a happy-go-lucky horn blower, like a lot of the musicians, no business ability or nothing. And so she put it down to him like it was and everything, but she got him away from Joe Oliver.
That's what Earl Hines -- Earl Hines told me, the day that Louis died, -- I interviewed him when he was in town --
Yeah.
And he said he and Louis were a couple of young Turks, they'd get through at the Sunset, and Louis always kept his mouthpiece in his pocket.
Right, right.
And they'd go out and sit in, --
Right, right, right.
-- and play until dawn.

Right, right, right, right. And then, like I told you about the baseball games, they used to get out in the park, come out there and play baseball. And I mean, it was just that type of a thing. But somewhere down the line, somebody had to take care of business. So Lil was the one that did it. She took care of business and he helped teach him to read and all of that, because he was as blind as a bat.
Yeah. And then when he left her, Johnny Collins, --
Yeah, Collins.
Who was a crook, as far as I can gather, --
Right, right, right.
And he sort of (unintelligible).
Well, he come back from Europe.
Then Joe Glaser took over.
Yeah, took over, right.
Like Lil had done.

Right, right, right. And, see, and then the different women, he had different wives and things. Right, so -- but during all of this, Lil still was faithful -- I mean, not faithful, but she loved him. She loved him til the end.
It's --
And we often said, well, I guess Lil's happy, she died doing a tribute to Louis Armstrong. And that's what it was, a tribute to him.
Like you said, that to me is a beautiful way to go.
Right, right, right, right, right.
And those pictures you showed me of her, right before she collapsed; she was radiant.
Right, right, right, right, right. See, and that was like at the Club DeLisa, at one of the celebrity night things, and he would be out there and she'd
come and they were just buddy-buddy, although they weren't married at that time any longer.
It's a relationship similar to Jimmy and Marion McPartland.
Right, right, right.
I guess they're better friends now since they've been divorced than they were when they were married.
That's true.
And she helps him.
Right, right, right.
But --

Yeah. All I can say is, and all of these stories and all of this reminiscing and all this talking and everything, only fortifies what I said before. I wouldn't give you anything for the 50 years that I've had in the business here in Chicago. Chicago has been good to me and the people here have been good to me. So, I mean, you can't ask for anything more than that, because so many guys have been out on the road and in tragic endings and whatnot. But, me, it's just been a beautiful story all the way through. I mean, it's a love story. Love with the city and the people, you know?
Well, you've done a lot for Chicago, too.

Well, I mean, whatever I did, it wasn't intentional -- I mean, intentionally for the purpose of doing it. I just wanted to do something for the people, because I run into so many beautiful people. Well, like you, Don, I've known you all through the DownBeat years and all of that, and you've always been great.
About 20 years.
Right, right, see, so -- and when you get friendships that last that long, you're saying something, you know?
Well, that's a good note to end on.
Oh, beautiful.
It's a beautiful B-flat .
Okay.
